muscles.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass of the forearm.
synonyms: extensor radialis longus + extensor radialis brevis (Straus 1941a,b)
extensor carpi radialis (Abdala & Moro 2006; Abdala et al. 2008)
extensor radialis superficialis + extensor carpi intermedius + extensor radialis profundus (Haines 1939; Walker 1973)
extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis (mammals)
abductor radialis (Meers 2003; Burch 2014, for the intermedius + profundus part)

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus and the adjacent supracondylar ridge.
consensus.insertion: Radius, proximal carpals, or (in mammals and some anurans) the metacarpals.
consensus.action: Extends the wrist and abducts (radially deviates) the manus; contributes to elbow extension.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The proximoventral ridge of the radius, present here and in Pederpes and read by Bishop (2014) in Ossinodus as the extensor carpi radialis insertion. No origin is scored: the ectepicondyle carries the forearm extensors as a group, and Molnar et al. do not divide that group between individual muscles in this taxon — the forearm extensors as a mass are among their highest-confidence reconstructions, the individual muscles within it are not.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. The proximoventral ridge of the radius (Bishop 2014), one of the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct fairly confidently here. See the brachioradialis row for why the two radial insertions may be one continuous field of scarring.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.note: Includes the extensor radialis longus + brevis sensu Straus (1941a,b).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Plesiomorphic tetrapod condition: insertion stops at the radius and proximal carpals.
occurrences.origin: Proximal part of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Almost the whole anterolateral surface of the radius, and the lateral surface of the radiale.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.note: In Phyllomedusa and other grasping tree frogs the insertion shifts distally onto the metacarpals, convergently with mammals.
occurrences.attachmentNote: In Phyllomedusa and other grasping tree frogs the insertion has shifted distally onto the metacarpals — the same shift mammals made, independently.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.note: Very likely includes the 'extensor metacarpi radialis' and the 'supinator' sensu Meyers (1996).

occurrences.name: Extensor metacarpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. Two heads, both on the processus supracondylaris dorsalis of the humerus — pars ventralis from its ventral surface, pars dorsalis from its dorsal surface, the latter itself two fused bellies separable along their whole length including the tendons. They fuse proximally into one bipennate belly. The common tendon passes through a groove at the distal radius and around the os radiale to insert on the processus extensorius of the carpometacarpus. The radiale is a pulley here, not an attachment, so it gets no row.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus + brevis
occurrences.action: Extends and abducts the hand at the wrist.
occurrences.note: The distal shift of insertion from carpus to metacarpus is a mammalian derived condition.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Distal migration onto the metacarpals, correlated with finer digital control — and convergent with the anuran condition.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the crista supraectepicondylaris, a crest along the proximal border of the ectepicondylus of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon passing under the abductor pollicis longus and under a transverse retinaculum binding it to the distal radius, then splitting into three branches onto the dorsal bases of metacarpals II-IV; the branch to metacarpal III is thickest and that to IV is sometimes absent.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. **The insertion is symmetrical about metacarpal III**, the mid-axis of the metacarpus, and Gambaryan et al. list that symmetry among the primitive monotreme features. They draw a homology conclusion from it: a muscle centred like this is comparable with the REPTILIAN extensor digitorum communis — the humerodorsalis of Haines (1939), already a synonym on `extensor-digitorum` — rather than with the reptilian extensor carpi radialis, which ends more proximally and preaxially. The rows stay on this record; see its homology block.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the proximal and preaxial borders of the ectepicondylus.
occurrences.insertion: As in the long-beaked echidna, but the branch to metacarpal II is considerably thinner and that to metacarpal IV is absent — though Haines (1939) described one.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. A disagreement with Haines over whether the fourth branch exists, kept because the record's own homology note says the interesting variable on this muscle is the level and spread of its insertion rather than its presence.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Ventral surface of the ectepicondylus parallel to its proximal border, deeper than the extensor digitorum communis.
occurrences.insertion: Three terminal branches onto the dorsal bases of metacarpals II-IV. The tendon passes under the abductor pollicis longus but over that muscle's transverse branch, and there is no transverse retinaculum binding it to the radius as there is in both echidnas.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The full three-branch insertion is retained here where the short-beaked echidna has lost the fourth; the retinaculum that holds the tendon down in Tachyglossidae is absent.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis and abductor radialis
occurrences.action: Extends and adducts the wrist; abductor radialis abducts and slightly flexes the forearm.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). Two of Burch's muscles land on this one homology group: his Extensor carpi radialis, and his Abductor radialis, which Walker (1973) and Russell & Bauer (2008) call extensor carpi radialis intermedius and profundus — already in this record's synonymy. Both arise from the ectepicondyle in close proximity.

**The extensor carpi radialis origin is the mirror image of the supinator problem and is resolved the same way**: proximal in birds (extreme enough in some to build a Processus supracondylaris dorsalis for it), between supinator and extensor digitorum longus in turtles, lepidosaurs and crocodylians. The proximal avian shift lets slight elbow extension fully extend the manus (Vazquez 1994), so it evolved with the wrist and was not present here. **The insertion is scored on the radiale on osteology rather than phylogeny**: birds insert on the carpometacarpus near the base of metacarpal I, lepidosaurs and crocodylians on the radiale, and *Tawa*'s wrist is plesiomorphic and more lepidosaur-like than either extant archosaur's, so the plesiomorphic insertion is inferred. Abductor radialis is the radius row: its insertion is equivocal because it fuses distally to extensor carpi radialis in birds, and if unfused in basal theropods it would have taken the proximal half of the lateral radius, stabilising as it does in crocodylians. It is absent in birds and single-bellied in crocodylians against two parts in lepidosaurs and some turtles — a general archosaurian reduction, which is what makes the single belly unequivocal even where its insertion is not.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
occurrences.action: Extends the wrist and abducts the hand.
occurrences.innervation: Radial nerve (longus); deep branch of the radial nerve (brevis).
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Longus from the lower third of the lateral supracondylar ridge to the base of the second metacarpal; brevis from the common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle to the base of the third. **This is the distal insertion shift the record is built around.** Turtles, lepidosaurs and crocodylians stop at the radius and proximal carpals; mammals and some grasping tree frogs have carried the insertion out onto the metacarpals independently, and Abdala & Diogo tie that shift to fine digital control. The human row is the mammalian end of a convergence, not evidence of a shared derived state.

**Extensor carpi radialis longus** (Gest). Lower third of the lateral supracondylar ridge to the base of the second metacarpal.

**Extensor carpi radialis brevis** (Gest). Common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle to the base of the third metacarpal. The pair differ by one metacarpal and by where on the humerus they start, and the longus origin above the epicondyle is what makes it a flexor of the elbow as well.

occurrences.name: M. extensor metacarpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Origin only — this is Part 1, which stops at the humerus. One of four muscles Matsuoka & Hasegawa figure arising from sharp depressions on the dorsal surface of the distal humerus, the avian epicondylus dorsalis, scored here as the lateral epicondyle. **The proximal position of this origin is a derived avian feature**: Burch (2014) argues the bird arrangement, in which extensor carpi radialis takes the most proximal place on the epicondyle and the supinator drops distally, evolved with the automating mechanism of the wing, and reconstructs the inverse for basal theropods.

occurrences.name: M. extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Two heads: the proximal with a tendinous ectepicondylar origin partly shared with the extensor digitorum longus, the second arising from the fascial sheath investing the first for three quarters of its length — a sheath that also gives origin to extensor digitorum longus fibres. Insertion along the anterior and mesial radius, the anterior part beginning just distal to the biceps and brachialis insertions and the mesial reaching as far proximally as the radial shaft goes, lateral to the supinator longus insertion. **This is the plesiomorphic radial insertion**, against the metacarpal insertion mammals and some tree frogs reached independently.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). A large cross-sectional origin on the cranial epicondyle of the humerus, a belly reduced distally, and a wide tendon crossing the wrist laterally to the distal half of the radius and the radial carpal bone. **No division into heads**: Moro & Abdala (2004, 2006) and Casals et al. (2012) find three — superficialis, intermedium and profundus — in *Tupinambis*, *Polychrus*, *Liolaemus* and *Phymaturus*, and Freitas et al. report the undivided condition here, agreeing with Zaaf et al. (1999) on the two geckos. Russell & Bauer, dissecting the same animal, describe two heads, the second from the fascial sheath investing the first.

occurrences.name: M. extensor carpi radialis brevis and longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Brevis arises with the supinator from the tip of the epicondylus radialis humeri and the elbow capsule, separates from it at mid-forearm and resolves into an aponeurosis onto the proximal end of metacarpal I; longus is the deep-layer member. **Metacarpal, not radius** — which is the distal insertion this record treats as the interesting variable, reached independently in mammals and some anurans, and here already present in a lepidosaur.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis longior and brevior
occurrences.divisionNote: Separate throughout in the large male thylacine; in the female the fleshy bellies were amalgamated and only the tendons distinct.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Separate throughout in the large male, amalgamated in the female** — Cunningham dissected both and says so, which makes this one of the few within-species observations in the report. In both animals the tendons were separate. Origin from the lateral supracondylar ridge below the supinator longus; insertions into the dorsal aspect of the bases of the second and third metacarpals. Cunningham's general remark is that the radial extensors are usually amalgamated in marsupials and that even where separate they tend towards fusion.

occurrences.name: Radial extensor (single)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. **The two radial extensors are one muscle here**, the fleshy bellies completely amalgamated, with two separate tendons to the dorsal aspect of the bases of the second and third metacarpals. Origin from the lateral supracondylar ridge below the supinator longus.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis longior and brevior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Separate along their whole length, and the brevior is large, powerful and **arises by three heads — an origin Cunningham says he has not seen in any other marsupial**: from the upper part of the lateral epicondyle; from the tendinous expansion on the surface of the supinator brevis; and from the posterior border of the radius below the supinator brevis. So two of its three heads are on the forearm rather than the humerus, one of them on another muscle's aponeurosis. It inserts on the radial border of the third metacarpal shaft a little beyond the base; the longior comes off the lower third of the supracondylar ridge to the radial border of the second metacarpal about its middle. Both have moved distally along the metacarpal from the base.

occurrences.name: Extensor metacarpi radialis
occurrences.note: Two bellies forming the anterior edge of the forewing musculature. The pars palmaris is twice the size of the pars anconalis. M. tensor patagii brevis inserts widely on the originating tendon of the anconalis part, and Fisher & Goodman suggest one of the two anconalis tendons may have been usurped from that insertion — in one specimen the origin was by a single tendon.
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955). Both parts arise from the ectepicondylar prominence, the palmaris proximal and palmar to the anconalis. Their calcified tendons fuse at the distal end of the radius into one uncalcified tendon, which crosses the anterior surface of the wrist and attaches to the proximal side of the tip of the **extensor process of metacarpal II** — the processus extensorius of the carpometacarpus, scored as the bone with `side: proximal` because the process is not yet a landmark record. Just before attaching it fuses with the inserting tendon of M. extensor longus digiti II.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. extensor carpi radialis.** This large muscle contains two distinct bellies. The more proximal belly originates from the proximal dorsal epicondyle but has an additional origin from the dorsal humerus at approximately two thirds of the way down the humeral shaft. A pit on the proximal dorsal epicondyle is associated with the main origin, but no correlate exists for the origin on the humeral shaft. The more distal belly has a long tendon of origin from the proximal dorsal epicondyle immediately adjacent to the tendon for the first belly, which widens into a fleshy belly at approximately one fourth of the way down the radial shaft. At approximately halfway down the length of the radius, the bellies fuse, and the muscle thins into a very long tendon. The tendon passes over the distal end of the radius to insert on the proximodorsal base of the proximal bony spur of the carpometacarpus, equivalent to the position of the extensor process in taxa that lack such spurs. A long transverse scar is associated with this muscle's insertion and that of Mm. propatagialis and extensor longus alulae on either side.

homology.notes: A stable row across all six reptile/amphibian columns plus mammals. The interesting variable is not presence but the proximodistal level of insertion, which shifted distally independently in mammals and in some anurans.
homology.teaching: Ties directly to Abdala & Diogo's finding that distal insertion shifts track fine digital control, and that mammals are not unique in achieving it.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 13 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis, in Timon.

muscles.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
synonyms: extensor carpi ulnaris (Walker 1973; Abdala et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Ulna, ulnare, or metacarpal V.
consensus.action: Extends the wrist and adducts (ulnarly deviates) the manus.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Scored on the posterior ulna with no landmark, deliberately. The posterior ulnar crest is present, and its appearance together with the olecranon is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of this muscle from the triceps at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda — but in crown tetrapods the crest is identified as the BOUNDARY between the dorsal and ventral forearm musculature rather than as an attachment, so naming it as the insertion would assert more than the source does.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: The postaxial mirror of the extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis, taking the distal part of the same epicondyle where that muscle takes the proximal part.
occurrences.origin: Distal part of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Posterolateral face of the ulna, and the ulnare and intermedium.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Arises from the radial (lateral) epicondyle despite acting on the ulnar side, its fibres crossing to insert along most of the extensor surface of the ulna and onto the ulnare and pisiform. **The only extensor acting on the ulnar side of the forearm in *Pseudemys***, and the triceps insertion partly separates it from the flexor carpi ulnaris on the other face of the same bone.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: = extensor carpi ulnaris + anconeus quartus sensu Holmes (1977).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Extensor carpi ulnaris from the ulnar condyle and proximal ulna, mainly onto the ulnare with a small expansion to the first metacarpal. In Gekko the insertion is restricted to the pisiform — a different carpal, and one of the clearest attachment differences between the two species.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Confusingly called flexor ulnaris by Meers (2003) despite being a dorsal-mass, radial-innervated muscle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus, reported as extensor carpi ulnaris: tendinous from the lateral condyle of the disto-ventral humerus to 'the dorsal manus'. NO INSERTION ROW, which reads correctly as not recorded. Klinkhamer et al. state that muscles inserting into the manus and pes were SEVERED DURING SKINNING and that for those muscles they 'left the description more general, simply describing insertion as into the manus/pes' — so the phrase is a record of a lost attachment, not a coarse one, and choosing a carpal or a metacarpal from it asserts what they were careful not to. This row previously read `metacarpals`.

occurrences.name: Extensor metacarpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A stout tendon on the dorsal epicondyle of the humerus, just distal to the common origin of the supinator and the extensor digitorum communis. The belly runs the length of the ulna and its tendon passes around the dorsal condyle of the ulna into the manus, inserting at the proximal end of the major metacarpal on its caudodorsal surface.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.action: Extends and adducts the hand at the wrist.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Extensor carpi ulnaris from the laterodistal humeral ectepicondyle and the articular capsule, onto the lateral base of metacarpal V and the craniolateral base of the accessory carpal.

occurrences.name: Extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: = extensor carpi ulnaris + anconeus quartus sensu Holmes (1977).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. **Insertion restricted to the pisiform**, where Eublepharis inserts mainly on the ulnare with a small expansion to metacarpal I. A different carpal bone in the two geckos — the sharpest single argument in this dataset against reading one lizard as Lepidosauria.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Two heads. The humeral head from the apex of the ectepicondylus by an inner-side aponeurosis shared with the extensor digitorum communis and lateralis; the ulnar head from the anterior aspect of the ulna at the level of the proximal end of the radius.
occurrences.insertion: The two heads fuse at the midlength of the antebrachium into a common tendon which passes under a transverse retinaculum at the distal end of the ulna and inserts on digit V by two branches — a proximal one on the postaxial side of its metacarpophalangeal joint and a distal one on the preaxial side of its proximal interphalangeal joint. Distal to the ulnare the tendon is underlaid by a collagen-adipose pad.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Gambaryan et al. list the extremely distal insertion of this muscle, almost reaching the end of digit V, among the ADVANCED monotreme features — a wrist extensor that has become a digital one.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Humeral head from the apex of the ectepicondylus, expanding onto its dorsal side, by the inner-side aponeurosis shared with the extensor digitorum communis and lateralis; ulnar head from the anterior aspect of the olecranon up to the level of the proximal end of the radius.
occurrences.insertion: The two heads converge bipennately on a common aponeurosis and the tendon passes under a transverse retinaculum at the end of the ulna to insert extremely distally, on the base of the ungual phalanx of digit V, postaxial to the extensor digitorum lateralis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The most distal of the three: this one reaches the terminal phalanx.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: One head only, the humeral: a fleshy origin on the apex of the ectepicondylus slightly aided by the aponeurosis shared with the extensor digitorum lateralis and communis.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon under the transverse retinaculum at the distal end of the ulna, together with the extensor digitorum lateralis tendon, splitting in the metacarpal region into four branches: three insert in cascade on the postaxial side of the three joints of digit V, and the most proximal thin one deviates postaxially to join the interosseus V lateralis on the outer side of metacarpal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **The ulnar head is gone** — both echidnas have two heads and the platypus one, so the division is polymorphic within Monotremata and the clade computes as `variable`. A muscle branch ending on another muscle rather than on bone is also worth noting: the fourth branch joins the interosseus.
occurrences.divisionNote: Single against `heads` in both echidnas, on the loss of the caput ulnare.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.action: Extends and abducts the wrist; slightly extends the forearm.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Half the bracket is missing by Burch's own decision.** Crocodylians have a dorsal-division muscle from the middle of the ectepicondyle inserting on the base of metacarpal II, which Meers (2003) called extensor carpi ulnaris and earlier workers (Ribbing 1907; Haines 1939; Cong et al. 1998) homologised with extensor digitorum longus. Burch adopts the earlier reading and codes extensor carpi ulnaris **absent in crocodylians**, so this reconstruction is bracketed by birds and lepidosaurs only. His argument is the direction of the insertion shift: paleognaths insert on the lateralmost metacarpal (III), as lepidosaurs do, and many neognaths on metacarpal II, so the lateralmost metacarpal is plesiomorphic and the crocodylian metacarpal-II insertion looks derived — or belongs to another muscle.

Insertion on the lateralmost metacarpal is therefore unequivocal (0.650 at the base of Aves, with a reversal to metacarpal III in Passeriformes at 0.934); insertion on any carpal is equivocal, and the pisiform row is inferred because *Tawa* still has a pisiform, as lepidosaurs do. Burch's prediction: when the pisiform was lost in the theropod wrist this muscle lost that insertion and kept the metacarpal one, which is the state some birds are in. A secondary tendon of origin from the proximal ulna, seen in some birds, is very unlikely here (0.040).

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.action: Extends the wrist and adducts the hand.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common extensor tendon and the middle half of the posterior border of the ulna, to the medial side of the base of the fifth metacarpal — insertion on the lateralmost metacarpal, which Burch (2014) argues is the plesiomorphic archosaur state too. **The name is a hazard on this record and the human row is the least confusing instance of it**: Meers calls the crocodylian muscle flexor ulnaris, Burch reassigns that name to the anconeus and codes extensor carpi ulnaris absent in crocodylians altogether. In a human it is an extensor by mass, by nerve and by action, with nothing arguing otherwise.

occurrences.name: M. extensor metacarpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Origin only, and **it is on the ventral side** — Matsuoka & Hasegawa place it with the two pronators among the three muscles leaving sharp depressions on the ventral surface of the distal humerus, the entepicondyle. The mirror of the flexor carpi ulnaris row on this same specimen, which arises dorsally: in this swan the two carpal ulnar muscles have swapped the sides their names imply. Elsewhere this muscle is an ectepicondylar extensor — Burch (2014) puts it among the most distal muscles on the ectepicondyle in *Tawa*, and codes it absent in crocodylians altogether.

occurrences.name: M. extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Humeral head by a stout flat tendon along the line running proximally from the dorsal ectepicondyle; ulnar head from the anterior olecranon just distal to the triceps insertion. Insertion on the ventrolateral shaft of metacarpal V with a proximal side branch onto the proximolateral dorsal surface of the pisiform, and some contribution to the flexor carpi ulnaris insertion. **Lateralmost metacarpal plus pisiform is exactly the state Burch (2014) reconstructs for *Tawa*** on the lepidosaur pattern, having coded this muscle absent in crocodylians altogether — so the lizard row is the evidence that reconstruction rests on.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Large and broad, lying medially on the zeugopodium, from the cranial epicondyle of the humerus to the shaft of the ulna. The cranial epicondyle is the ectepicondyle: Freitas et al. equate their cranial epicondyle with the crocodilian origin Meers (2003) describes, and Russell & Bauer's rows for this same animal carry the extensors on the ectepicondyle and the flexors and pronators on the entepicondyle, so the identification is the dataset's existing one and not a fresh inference. Freitas et al. side with Abdala & Diogo (2010) against Meers on what the muscle does — extension of the limb rather than flexion. Russell & Bauer add an ulnar head from the anterior olecranon that Freitas et al. do not report.

occurrences.name: M. extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. From the epicondylus radialis humeri to the lateralmost metacarpal — the insertion Burch (2014) argues is plesiomorphic for archosaurs too, against the metacarpal-II insertion of many neognaths. Note that Burch codes this muscle absent in crocodylians altogether on his reading of Meers, so the lepidosaur row is one of the two halves his reconstruction rests on.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.divisionNote: Two distinct factors in the large male thylacine, one undivided muscle in the female. Both animals were dissected by Cunningham.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Split into two distinct muscles in the large male, single in the female** — the clearest within-species variation Cunningham records. In the male the two factors insert respectively into the unciform bone and the ulnar face of the base of the fifth metacarpal; in the female a single muscle reaches the fifth metacarpal alone. Scored `variable` for that reason, with the male's two insertions carried in the attachment rows. Cunningham's five-compartment extensor retinaculum in the thylacine and seven-compartment one in the cuscus are the tally of these tendons at the wrist.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Split into two factors as in the male thylacine, inserting into the unciform bone and the ulnar face of the base of the fifth metacarpal. This is the only muscle of the extensor forearm in which the phascogale is more divided than the cuscus.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. A single ulnar extensor inserted into the metacarpal of the minimus. Cunningham's five-compartment extensor retinaculum in the thylacine and seven-compartment one in the cuscus are the tally of these tendons at the wrist.

occurrences.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. extensor carpi ulnaris.** The tendon of origin is not visible in our CT dataset, but we confirmed that its origin is from the apex of the dorsal epicondyle, just proximal to that of M. ectepicondyloulnaris. There is no associated osteological correlate. The fleshy belly of the muscle lies superficial to the other muscles of the dorsal forearm. It narrows to a tendon at approximately two thirds down the length of the forearm, and is closely associated with the tendons of Mm. extensor longus digiti majoris and extensor digitorum communis, but can no longer be observed distal to the wrist in our CT data. We confirmed that it has a typical insertion on a raised scar on the dorsal carpometacarpus just proximal to the interosseous space.

homology.notes: Constant across Tetrapoda. Meers's (2003) 'flexor ulnaris' for the crocodylian muscle is a naming hazard, not a homology claim — the muscle is an extensor by mass, nerve and action.
homology.teaching: Good demonstration that a muscle's name may contradict its innervation and mass assignment; the nerve wins.

muscles.name: Extensor digitorum
synonyms: extensor digitorum longus (Abdala et al. 2008; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000; Meers 2003)

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aponeuroses of the digits.
consensus.action: Extends the digits, and secondarily the wrist.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: The most superficial forearm muscle in dorsal view. It serves digits II-IV only — the salamander manus has four digits, digit V having been lost.
occurrences.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal surfaces of the proximal phalanges of digits II, III and IV, by paired tendons.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Narrow origin on the radial (lateral) epicondyle, fanning over the forearm and dorsum of the hand, then dividing into four tongue-like processes that pass between the digits and subdivide into **eight slips** onto the sides of the distal end of each metacarpal — two per digit except digits I and V, which lack a slip on their outer surface. Almost vestigial in sea turtles, where the distal flipper has lost independent action.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Extensor digitorum longus, by tendon from the ulnar condyle onto the proximal ulnar side of metacarpals II-IV. Gekko has four distal tendinous branches inserting on both sides of metacarpals II-IV instead.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus americana, from Fisher & Goodman's Origin/Insertion paragraphs. M. extensor digitorum communis: tendinous from the most distal part of the face of the ectepicondylar prominence, with **a wide vinculum passing posteriorly from the distal end of that tendon to insert along a line on the postero-anconal corner of the ulna, just anterior to the row of papillae for the secondary feathers** — a second, aponeurotic attachment tied directly to the flight-feather apparatus. The round tendon runs distad along the antero-anconal ulna, through the tendinal groove at its distal end, onto the fused area of metacarpals III and IV.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A stout tendon on the dorsal epicondyle of the humerus, in common with the supinator. The tendon runs through a tendinal sulcus at the distal ulna, is bound to the dorsal surface of the alular metacarpal by a retinaculum, then bifurcates: the shorter branch inserts on the caudal surface of the proximal alula, the longer runs in a sulcus of the major metacarpal deep to the extensor longus digiti majoris and inserts on the craniodorsal surface of the proximal end of the first phalanx of the major digit. One row for both branches, because they are two ends of one tendon on one element.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.action: Extends the digits at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Extensor digitorum communis, from the distal ectepicondylar crest and tendinously near the humeral ectepicondyle, dividing into four principal tendons to the lateral digits. In three of six cases the belly was partly divided in its middle region.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Four distal tendinous branches inserting on **both sides** of metacarpals II-IV, where Eublepharis inserts only on the proximal ulnar side.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis + lateralis
occurrences.divisionNote: Panthera onca. The communis has two bellies, medial and lateral, in all three species. The LATERAL digital extensor is where they part company: one belly here, two in the ocelot and Geoffroy's cat, whose medial belly divides again into two tendons.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. Sanchez et al. describe the bellies and tendons rather than restating the epicondylar origin, which is the standard carnivoran one; the origin row is the lateral epicondyle on that basis and carries no landmark finer than the bone. In the jaguar and the ocelot the extensor digiti I and extensor digiti II arise from the proximal third of the ulnar diaphysis and each divides into two bellies — the digit I belly continuing as two tendons that fuse into an expansion at the distal phalanx, the digit II belly as a single tendon that fuses with the lateral extensor's tendon to the same digit.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis + lateralis
occurrences.divisionNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. FOUR bellies against the jaguar's three, because the lateral digital extensor is clearly divided in two here and its medial belly splits again into two tendons. The ocelot agrees with Geoffroy's cat, not with the jaguar.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. See the jaguar row; the attachments are the same and the difference is in how many bellies the lateral extensor holds.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the preaxial border of the ectepicondylus, deeper than the extensor carpi ulnaris and sharing its aponeurosis of origin; that aponeurosis also gives rise to the extensor digitorum lateralis.
occurrences.insertion: A flat terminal tendon passing under the retinaculum extensorum, expanding strongly on the dorsum of the manus and splitting into three branches to the ungual phalanges of digits II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. One of the three specimens carried the pre-mammalian condition as an individual variation: the extensor digitorum communis and the extensor digitorum profundus fused into a single tendon before branching, giving one extensor to all five digits with a humeral and an ulnar head. Gambaryan et al. treat that variant as a model of the ancestral integrity of the digital extensors, and the fibre slip that crosses between the two muscles in Tachyglossus as the other trace of it.

parts.name: Extensor digitorum lateralis
parts.note: Gambaryan et al. give it as Diogo & Abdala's (2010) extensor digiti minimi. Marked disputed because in all three genera its fibres arise from the extensor digitorum communis' own aponeurosis of origin rather than from bone, which is an argument that it is a differentiation of that muscle rather than an independent one. In Zaglossus, two of three specimens also had a fleshy origin directly on the ectepicondylus.

occurrences.divisionNote: The lateralis inserts on digits IV and V — in this genus onto the ungual phalanx of IV and the PREUNGUAL phalanx of V, whose ungual is reduced.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the distal-preaxial angle of the ectepicondylus, deeper than the extensor carpi ulnaris, by two superficial aponeuroses; the outer one is shared with the humeral head of the extensor carpi ulnaris and with the extensor digitorum lateralis, and forms a longitudinal trough housing the belly of the latter.
occurrences.insertion: Three main branches to digits II-IV, the branch to digit II sending a minor sub-branch to the ungual phalanx of digit I and the branch to digit IV a pair of sub-branches to the ungual phalanx of digit V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Some fibres split off the belly to join the extensor digitorum profundus, which is the second trace of the undivided ancestral extensor.
occurrences.divisionNote: The lateralis reaches the ungual phalanges of both digits IV and V here, where in the long-beaked echidna digit V takes only the preungual.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the ectepicondylus, ascending from the crest on its preaxial apex — where it arises under the extensor carpi ulnaris — along the whole proximal border, where it arises over the extensor carpi radialis. Two aponeuroses of origin, the outer shared with the extensor carpi ulnaris and the extensor digitorum lateralis.
occurrences.insertion: On the manus the terminal tendon divides into a superficial sheet splitting to the ungual phalanges of digits I-IV and a deep sheet splitting to those of digits II-IV; the long tendons also send short deep branches to the bases of the preungual phalanges and fuse dorsally with the interdigital tendons of the cutaneus trunci.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The dorsal digital tendons here are continuous with the skin muscle, which is a muscle end no correlate would record — the cutaneus trunci branches run out between the digits and insert on opposing sides of the claws.

parts.name: Extensor digitorum lateralis
parts.note: Rudimentary in this genus: a very thin tendon whose branches to digits IV and V thin out and fuse with the corresponding extensor digitorum communis tendons before insertion.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.action: Extends the wrist and the digits.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). The origin is the least contested thing in the antebrachium: approximately the middle of the ectepicondyle, between extensor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi radialis or supinator, at a proportional probability near 1.0 at every node.

**The insertion is a count of digits, and one of them is scored on function rather than phylogeny.** Slips to digits I and II are phylogenetically unequivocal — birds keep both, though on the base of phalanx I rather than the metacarpal. Everything else is equivocal: the digit V slip is lost in all lepidosaurs and archosaurs (0.995), the digit IV slip survives in lepidosaurs, turtles and *Alligator*, and metacarpal III is reported for *Crocodylus acutus*. *Tawa* has three functional digits and a highly reduced digit IV, so Burch infers the digit III insertion from the hand's own proportions and drops digit IV as probably already lost. That is extrapolatory functional inference, which Burch flags as the method that risks circularity if the result is later used to argue about function — he excludes ambiguous muscles from his own functional discussion for that reason.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum and extensor digiti minimi
occurrences.action: Extends the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints of digits 2-5; extends the wrist.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Both from the common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle; extensor digiti minimi joins the extensor digitorum tendon to the fifth digit rather than reaching bone on its own. **The insertion is not on a phalanx at all** — it is the extensor expansion, the fibrous hood over the dorsum of each digit that the intrinsic muscles also insert into, so the long extensor and the lumbricals and interossei act on the interphalangeal joints through one shared structure. In the outgroups this muscle ends on the bases of the metacarpals or on the terminal phalanges directly. The expansion is what replaces those attachments.

**Extensor digitorum** (Gest). Common extensor tendon to the extensor expansions of digits 2-5; the expansion then sends a central band to the middle phalanx and two slips to the distal one.

**Extensor digiti minimi** (Gest). Same origin, joining the extensor digitorum tendon to the fifth digit. Gest calls it the ulnar-most portion of extensor digitorum, which is the source's own reason for the two being one record.

occurrences.name: M. extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Origin only. The second of the four dorsal depressions on the distal humerus. In every taxon Burch surveyed this muscle arises from about the middle of the ectepicondyle between the carpal extensors, at a proportional probability near 1.0 at every node — one of the few attachments in the forelimb that does not move.

occurrences.name: M. extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Origin immediately dorsal to the radial condyle of the humerus by a short tendon closely applied to the joint capsule, with accessory fibres from the intermuscular septum against the extensor carpi radialis. Three tendons: the lateralmost to the proximolateral dorsal surface of metacarpal IV, the middle to the head of metacarpal III, the medialmost to metacarpal II — each passing between the short digital extensors of the two digits it lies between. **Three metacarpals, not five**, which is the state Burch (2014) reconstructs for *Tawa* on functional grounds and finds unequivocal only for digits I and II across the archosaur bracket.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Fusiform with parallel fibres in the middle of the zeugopodium, from the cranial epicondyle of the humerus, its broad dorsal tendon dividing into three long thin tendons to the distal phalanges of digits I, II and III. **The insertion is the finding.** Freitas et al. set it against a reptilian norm of insertion on the metacarpal bases — II in crocodilians, II–IV in the geckos and the tegu, II, III and V in *Polychrus* — and against Russell & Bauer, whose *Iguana* row inserts on the metacarpals. A phalangeal insertion is otherwise mostly an avian character; they read the distal attachment as improving grip in a climbing animal, where the proximal one suits terrestrial locomotion. In crocodilians this muscle is named extensor carpi ulnaris longus (Meers 2003; Abdala & Diogo 2010), a difference Freitas et al. call purely conceptual since function and topography agree.

occurrences.name: M. extensor digitorum communis longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *epicondylo-metacarpalis medius*. Same origin as the extensor carpi radialis brevis, descending the middle of the extensor surface and splitting on the dorsum of the hand into four tendinous slips, each to the ulnar side of the base of metacarpals I to IV. **Four metacarpals** — against three functional digits in *Tawa*, where Burch reconstructs slips to I-III on the hand's own proportions.

occurrences.name: Extensor communis digitorum and extensor digitorum secundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The common extensor is comparatively small in all three animals. Here its belly divides high in the forearm into three slips giving three tendons, and **each tendon then splits in two on the dorsum of the hand**: the first serves index and medius, the second medius and annularis, the third annularis and minimus — so the two middle digits get two slips each and the outer two get one. The extensor digitorum secundus, which Cunningham calls the representative of the human extensor digiti minimi, is essentially the same in all three: from the lateral epicondyle, its tendon splitting to the dorsal expansions of the annular and little digits.

occurrences.name: Extensor communis digitorum and extensor digitorum secundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The common extensor gives **four tendons**, communicating freely on the dorsum of the hand and going one to each of the four ulnar digits — the simpler arrangement, against the thylacine's three tendons splitting into six slips. Cunningham notes Young found a tendon to each of the five digits in the koala and calls that exceptional, the insertion being confined to the four inner digits in most marsupials. The extensor digitorum secundus is as in the thylacine, to the annular and little digits; Macalister has it reaching the medius as well in the Tasmanian devil and the two kangaroos.

occurrences.name: Extensor communis digitorum and extensor digitorum secundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. The common extensor gives **four tendons**, communicating freely on the dorsum of the hand and going one to each of the four ulnar digits — the simpler arrangement, against the thylacine's three tendons splitting into six slips. Cunningham notes Young found a tendon to each of the five digits in the koala and calls that exceptional, the insertion being confined to the four inner digits in most marsupials. The extensor digitorum secundus is as in the thylacine, to the annular and little digits; Macalister has it reaching the medius as well in the Tasmanian devil and the two kangaroos.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. extensor digitorum communis.** The origin is by a relatively thick tendon to the proximal cranial side of the dorsal epicondyle that is closely associated with but separate from the M. supinator tendon of origin. There is no corresponding osteological correlate for the insertion. The fleshy belly of the muscle extends approximately one third the length of the radius, and lies deep to M. extensor carpi ulnaris for much of its length. The tendon of insertion crosses the wrist in close association with those of Mm. extensor carpi ulnaris and extensor longus digiti majoris, but cannot be observed in the CT dataset distal to this point, likely due to thick overlying connective tissue that prevented the uptake of stain. We confirmed that the tendon of insertion splits, with one branch inserting on the caudal edge of the alular phalanx and the other passing through the tendinal groove on the dorsal carpometacarpus to insert on the proximalmost cranial edge of phalanx I of the major digit, where it leaves a tiny impression.

homology.notes: Universal across limbed tetrapods; one of the least contested rows in Table 1 despite six different names.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 13 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the extensor digitorum.

muscles.name: Extensores digitorum breves
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass, intrinsic to the manus.
synonyms: extensores digiti brevis (Abdala et al. 2008; Abdala & Moro 2006)
extensores breves superficiales + extensores breves medii (Gaupp 1896)

consensus.origin: Distal radius/ulna, carpals, and metacarpals — dorsal surface.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aponeuroses of the digits.
consensus.action: Extends the digits; fine positional control independent of the long extensor.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Serves digits II-IV, matching the extensor digitorum communis and reflecting the four-digit salamander manus.
occurrences.origin: Carpals at the bases of digits II, III and IV.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal surface of the proximal end of the terminal phalanx of each digit, by long tendons.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: The extensor indicis brevis superficialis arises continuously from the radiale and the short ligament joining radiale and ulnare, lateral to the extensor carpi radialis tendon that attaches to element Y.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Five, on the dorsum of the hand deep to the extensor digitorum communis, arising more or less in common from the ulnare and adjacent carpal elements and ending in small tendons on the penultimate phalanges; those to the middle three digits pass between the insertion slips of the communis. **Absent in most testudinines**, reduced to the first digit in Pelomedusa, and present for the first three in Geochelone elephantopus — a series that tracks how much independent digital movement the animal has.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the ulnare onto the distalmost phalanx of digits I-V. In Gekko the insertion is on the antepenultimate phalanx except digit I, where it is the first phalanx.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.note: Attachment rows for this taxon describe the foot and have been moved to the pes record.

Rattus norvegicus, the mammal in Abdala & Diogo's Tables 2 and 3. Largely lost or reduced in the therian manus, though a dorsal intrinsic layer persists in some taxa; they note that the reduction of the intrinsic hand musculature is a mammalian trend, not a mammalian elaboration.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Inserts on the **antepenultimate** phalanx of digits II-V and on the first phalanx of digit I, against the distalmost phalanx throughout in Eublepharis. Scored without a side: the dataset has no vocabulary for position along a digit.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.action: Extends the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **The insertion is unequivocal and *Tawa* has the scar; the origins of the superficial layer are the guess.** Each digit gets a superficialis and a profundus belly which join into one tendon on the dorsal surface of the proximal end of the terminal phalanx — and *Tawa* carries an oval, lightly striated area on the dorsal surface of all three manual unguals. Profundus origins are conserved everywhere: each belly from its own metacarpal, extending onto the base of the metacarpal medial to it. Superficialis origins are not: crocodylians spread them across the proximal carpals rather than confining them to the ulnare, intermedium or distal ulna as turtles and lepidosaurs do, so the lateral divisions are conserved and the medial ones are not. Burch reads the avian manus back onto this and puts the digit I and II divisions on the radiale, the digit III and IV divisions on the ulnare.

The avian evidence he is reading is a chain of homologies: Extensor brevis alulae is profundus of digit I (the avian extensor process being embryologically metacarpal I — Kundrát 2009); Extensor longus digiti majorus is the two divisions of digit II, its proximal belly arising from the radius as in no other taxon but most closely aligned with the crocodylian radiale origin; and Ulnimetacarpalis dorsalis is a short extensor rather than the abductor digiti minimi that Diogo & Abdala (2010) make it, on the grounds that it derives from the dorsal division while abductor digiti minimi runs with the flexors. Bellies to the reduced digit IV are reconstructed rather than dropped, because crocodylians keep small ones on their reduced fifth digit — though the profundus belly of digit IV may have ended on the metacarpal rather than the ungual, as it does in crocodylians, which is why no metacarpal insertion row is asserted.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **Absent, and the absence is worth a row.** Gest lists 54 muscles of the upper limb and no short dorsal digital extensor among them; the human hand has no extensor digitorum brevis manus as a normal structure, though it is a recognised variant. Every other amniote column on this record has one. The foot kept its equivalent — see `extensores-digitorum-breves-pes`, where the human extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis are scored — so this is a loss in the hand specifically, in the limb that became a manipulator.

occurrences.name: Mm. extensores digitores breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **All five superficial slips arise from the ulnare alone** — a single carpal serving every digit — and fan out in a stratified fashion, the largest to digit V, then digit I. The profundi arise from the dorsal metacarpal of the digit each serves. The two layers' tendons combine and insert middorsally on the proximal end of each ungual phalanx, with a small sesamoid in the common tendon dorsal to the distalmost joint. Russell & Bauer note that the slips to digits I and II have often been given separate names by analogy with the mammalian hand — Romer's adductor pollicis longus and extensor indicis proprius — which is the same borrowing that put a human name on a lizard muscle elsewhere in this dataset. Compare Burch's *Tawa* reconstruction, which puts the digit I and II superficial slips on the radiale and III and IV on the ulnare from avian evidence; *Iguana* puts all of them on the ulnare.

occurrences.name: M. extensor digitorum communis brevis
occurrences.innervation: R. dorsalis of the N. radialis profundus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Osawa's muscle 43, on the dorsum of the hand. All the short extensors end on the basal phalanx of their digit and then pass into its dorsal aponeurosis, which is why Osawa says they are all to be regarded as extensors — the same extensor-expansion arrangement the human hand uses, in an animal that has kept five digits.

homology.notes: A conserved dorsal intrinsic layer of the manus across non-mammalian tetrapods. Its reduction in mammals is part of the broader loss of intrinsic hand muscles that Abdala & Diogo highlight.
homology.teaching: Supporting evidence for the claim that human hands have fewer intrinsic muscles than lizard or salamander hands.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 13 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the extensores digitorum breves.

muscles.name: Abductor pollicis longus
synonyms: abductor et extensor digiti I (Brooks 1889; Ribbing 1907; Howell 1936a,b; Straus 1941a,b)
abductor indicis longus (Gaupp 1896; Manzano et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Dorsal surface of the ulna and/or radius and the interosseous membrane.
consensus.insertion: Base of metacarpal I — or of the most radial metacarpal present.
consensus.action: Abducts and extends the first (most radial) digit; supinates the manus in sprawling taxa.

occurrences.name: Abductor et extensor digiti I
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. abductor et extensor digiti I. Wholly intrinsic to the hand — it takes no origin in the forearm, unlike the amniote abductor pollicis longus, which is why the name transfers badly.
occurrences.origin: Radiale and intermedium.
occurrences.insertion: Distal end of the first metacarpal.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.note: The key case. Adult anurans have lost digit 1, so the most radial digit is digit 2 — and the abductor pollicis longus homologue attaches to it. What determines the attachment is the POSITION of the digit (most radial), not its embryological identity.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rhinella arenarum. Insertion: Digit 2, not digit 1. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta. Origin: Ulna. Insertion: Metacarpal I. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis, the squamate name for this muscle: from the distal border of the ventral surface of the ulna onto the radial border of metacarpal I. Scored on the ulna without a landmark for the distal border, which is not a named process here.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.action: Abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Abductor digiti I longus: from the lateral surface of the ulnar AND radial diaphyses, its tendons held by a dedicated retinaculum in a groove at the craniomedial distal radius, inserting by two tendons at the first digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti I longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. A MORE PROXIMAL origin than in Geoffroy's cat, running along the whole lateral edge of the ulna, over the proximal two-thirds of the radius, and onto the interosseous membrane of the forearm. The membrane row matters: a third of this muscle's origin is not on bone at all, so the osteological correlate understates it. No insertion row — Sanchez et al. do not state where it ends in these species.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti I longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. The same three surfaces as the jaguar and the ocelot but a LESS PROXIMAL origin on the radius — the one difference Sanchez et al. draw for this muscle, and the reason the radius row here carries no `proximal` side where the jaguar's does. Scoring both species is what makes the difference visible; a single Theria row would have had to pick one.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.origin: Adjacent parts of the anterior sides of the radius and ulna, descending from the elbow joint over more than half the length of the radius.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon formed in the distal quarter of the antebrachium, running under its own transverse retinaculum in a groove on the distal end of the radius to the preaxial side of metacarpal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The groove on the distal radius is an osteological correlate for the tendon rather than for the muscle.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.origin: The ulna only. More postaxially the anterior surface of the ulna is taken by the extensor digitorum profundus, and the boundary between the two origins is marked on the bone by a rugosity.
occurrences.insertion: Distal aponeuroses on the inner and outer surfaces of the belly fuse into a terminal tendon passing under its own transverse retinaculum at the distal end of the radius to the preaxial side of metacarpal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The one genus whose abductor pollicis longus has left the radius entirely, and it leaves a readable boundary: a rugosity on the ulna separating it from the extensor digitorum profundus. Two muscles sharing a bone and marking where one stops.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.origin: Anterior side of the proximal end of the radius and the adjacent part of the ulna.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon under its own transverse retinaculum at the distal end of the radius to the preaxial side of the base of metacarpal I, giving off at the level of the wrist a postaxial branch which passes over the brachioradialis tendon, deeper than every other extensor tendon, to insert on the preaxial side of the ulnare.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The postaxial branch onto the ulnare is unique to this genus, and it is the structure that holds the brachioradialis tendon down in place of the sheath the echidnas use.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus
occurrences.action: Extends and abducts the wrist; abducts the first digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **The one origin in the antebrachium that is a synapomorphy rather than an inference.** Lepidosaurs and turtles take this muscle from the ulnar shaft alone; crocodylians and birds both add a head from the radius, making it bipennate, at a proportional probability of 0.955 at the archosaur node — so it originated from the facing (interosseous) surfaces of both bones in *Tawa*. No sides are scored on those two rows: Burch gives the origin as the facing surfaces, and which named face of each bone that is depends on the articulated position, which is not recorded. The radial head is reversed in Passeriformes and present in all other birds studied.

Insertion on the medial side of the base of metacarpal I is plesiomorphic and retained even in birds, where the alular extensor process of the carpometacarpus is developmentally part of metacarpal I (Kundrát 2009). Crocodylians do not share it — their tendon goes to the radiale — but phylogenetic inference puts that at 0.980 against, i.e. derived within the clade. *Tawa*, *Herrerasaurus* and other basal theropods have a medial flange at the base of metacarpal I in the right position for it.

occurrences.name: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
occurrences.action: Abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint; extensor pollicis brevis extends it at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Abductor pollicis longus from the middle third of the posterior radius, the interosseous membrane and the mid-posterolateral ulna, to the radial side of the base of the first metacarpal; extensor pollicis brevis from the membrane and the distal posterior radius to the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. **Both bones is the archosaur condition too** — Burch (2014) makes the two-headed origin from the facing surfaces of radius and ulna a synapomorphy of Archosauria at 0.955, against a purely ulnar origin in lepidosaurs and turtles, so humans and birds share a bipennate origin that is not shared by descent. Extensor pollicis brevis is scored as the second part of the group on this record's own synonymy, which names the muscle 'abductor et extensor digiti I'.

**Abductor pollicis longus** (Gest). Middle third of the posterior radius, the interosseous membrane and the mid-posterolateral ulna, to the radial side of the base of the first metacarpal.

**Extensor pollicis brevis** (Gest). Interosseous membrane and distal posterior radius to the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. With the abductor it makes the lateral border of the snuffbox, which is the clinical reason the two are learned together and no reason at all for their being one record — that is the shared origin field on the radius.

occurrences.name: M. supinator manus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). From the distal third of the dorsal ulna, crossing the distal antebrachium distomesially to insert by a single tendon on the dorsomesial aspect of the proximal end of metacarpal I. **The name on this record's synonym list, in the animal it was coined for** — 'supinator manus' is how Haines (1939), Walker (1973) and Holmes (1977) refer to the abductor pollicis longus, and Russell & Bauer add the developmental reading: although they discuss it among the dorsal antebrachial muscles, they judge it probably a muscle of the dorsal matrix of the manus that has migrated proximally. Ulna only — the radial head that makes the muscle bipennate is an archosaur synapomorphy Burch (2014) scores at 0.955, and this row is the lepidosaur state it is measured against.

occurrences.name: M. abductor et extensor pollicis longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. The deep-layer partner of the extensor carpi radialis longus, and this record's name in the lepidosaur literature — Haines, Walker and Holmes call it *supinator manus*, which Russell & Bauer use for the *Iguana* row scored here. Its origin from both forearm bones rather than the ulna alone is worth reading against Burch (2014), who makes the two-headed origin an archosaur synapomorphy at 0.955 measured against a purely ulnar lepidosaur condition.

occurrences.name: Extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. A very extensive origin — the extensor surfaces of both forearm bones in their upper two-thirds and the interosseous membrane between — dividing into two fleshy slips that emerge between the common extensor and the short radial extensor and end in tendons winding round the radial border of the forearm, one to the trapezium and one to the base of the first metacarpal. **Cunningham's identification is the one this record already carries**: he says plainly that the muscle in marsupials is a compound of the human extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis and extensor primi internodii pollicis, which is exactly the pair scored as parts on the human row here.

occurrences.name: Extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **The two portions are separable along their whole extent**, and they have different origins: the slip going to the metacarpal comes off the middle third of the radius, the slip going to the trapezium off the lower half of the ulna, the adjacent interosseous membrane and very slightly the radius. In the cuscus the same two slips share one origin. **Cunningham's identification is the one this record already carries**: he says plainly that the muscle in marsupials is a compound of the human extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis and extensor primi internodii pollicis, which is exactly the pair scored as parts on the human row here.

occurrences.name: Extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Very like the cuscus's but with a less extensive origin. **Cunningham's identification is the one this record already carries**: he says plainly that the muscle in marsupials is a compound of the human extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis and extensor primi internodii pollicis, which is exactly the pair scored as parts on the human row here.

homology.notes: Homology of the muscle is secure; what varies is which digit it lands on. Ribbing (1907) argued that Gaupp's (1896) anuran 'abductor pollicis' actually corresponds to the pronator quadratus rather than the abductor pollicis brevis — a caution that the anuran forearm nomenclature is unusually tangled.
homology.teaching: The flagship position-versus-identity example. Pair with the urodele abductor digiti minimi (digit 4) and the counter-case in chickens where digit identity does appear to matter.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 13 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the abductor pollicis longus, in Timon.

muscles.name: Brachioradialis
synonyms: tractor radii (Haines 1939; Walker 1973; Wyneken 2001; Abdala et al. 2008)
supinator (Burch 2014 — theropod usage, explicitly equated with Meers 2003 'supinator' and Walker 1973 'tractor radii')

consensus.origin: Lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Distal radius.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow; in mammals, brings the forearm to mid-pronation.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from the convex supinator process on the anterior edge of the humerus, two-thirds of the way along (Coates 1996); the identification of the muscle comes from Eryops, where the supinator process carries the 'supinator longus' (Miner 1925), and from captorhinids, not from this taxon. Insertion on the dorsomesial ridge of the radius, one of the four ridges Bishop (2014) read on the Ossinodus radius and which Molnar et al. report as present here and in Pederpes. Bishop found no break in the scarring between the dorsomesial and proximoventral ridges, so this insertion and the extensor carpi radialis's may not be separate.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. The dorsomesial ridge of the radius, read by Bishop (2014) as the insertion of the brachioradialis ('supinator longus'), with the caution he attaches: there is no break in the muscle scarring between this ridge and the proximoventral ridge, so this insertion and the extensor carpi radialis's may not be separate. Godfrey (1989) made the same kind of reading for the two mesial ridges of the Greererpeton radius, as the boundary between the extensor and flexor masses. Molnar et al. place the separation of the two muscles at Elpistostegalia, marked by a scar or facet distal to the supinator ridge.

occurrences.note: Not an independent muscle in Ambystoma.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.note: = tractor radii sensu Haines (1939), Walker (1973), Wyneken (2001).
Absent in Timon but seemingly present in Sphenodon.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.note: Appears to correspond to the 'supinator' sensu Meers (2003).
Marked '– [but see text]'.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.action: Flexes the elbow, strongest in mid-pronation.
occurrences.note: Anomalous among the radial-innervated group in being an elbow flexor rather than an extensor.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Supinator longus. From the humeral diaphysis immediately caudodistal to the brachialis origin, running up to the cranial surface of the ectepicondylar crest; origin length varied between specimens, in some reaching the proximal diaphysis near the humeral neck. Inserts on the craniomedial distal radius.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. From the proximal third of the CAUDAL surface of the humerus, covering the cranial forearm muscles, to insert medially at the distal end of the radius and on the proximal row of the carpus by a thick flattened tendon. The carpal row is the part worth noting: this record's consensus stops at the distal radius, and in these felids the tendon carries past it. Very well developed in the jaguar and the ocelot, much less so in Geoffroy's cat — the clearest of the size-related differences the paper reports.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the ventral surface of the ectepicondylus near its proximal border, deeper than the extensor carpi radialis.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon passing under the abductor pollicis longus onto the dorsal projection of the preaxial carpal complex, between its joints with distal carpals II and III; the tendon is held at the distal end of the radius by a connective-tissue sheath.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. **The insertion is not on the radius.** Everywhere else in this dataset the brachioradialis ends on the radius — that is what the name is about — and in all three monotreme genera it passes the radius entirely and ends on the fused radiale + intermedium + centrale, the preaxial carpal complex.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the ventral surface of the ectepicondylus along its proximal border, only the postaxial part of the origin passing under that of the extensor carpi radialis.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon passing under the abductor pollicis longus onto the dorsal projection of the preaxial carpal complex, between its joints with distal carpals II and III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Allen (1912) took the radial head of the brachialis for this muscle, which is worth noting because the two do lie together and the mistake is in the older literature the therian rows on this record descend from.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the ventral surface of the ectepicondylus clear of its proximal border, deeper than both the extensor carpi radialis and the extensor digitorum communis, which has expanded proximally along the ectepicondylar border.
occurrences.insertion: As in the echidnas, onto the preaxial carpal complex; the only real difference is that the tendon is bound to the distal end of the radius by a transverse branch of the abductor pollicis longus tendon rather than by its own sheath.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Same bone, different retaining structure — the tendon is held down by a neighbour's tendon instead of by a ligament of its own.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.action: Flexes and supinates the forearm.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Scored on this record, not on `supinator`, and the name is the reason to read the note.** Burch's Table 1 equates his Supinator with Meers's (2003) crocodylian 'Supinator' and Walker's (1973) chelonian 'Tractor radii' — which are the two synonyms this record already carries. The dataset's separate `supinator` record holds the therian muscle and the avian usage of the word, neither of which is this. A fourth source landing on the same equation is worth having on the record that already calls itself the worst name in the comparative forearm literature.

The insertion is as firm as anything in the paper: the anterolateral radial shaft for more than half its length, at 0.999, present in turtles, lepidosaurs, crocodylians and all but a handful of derived birds, and supported in *Tawa* by a flat anterior radial surface bounded by low ridges running the length of the bone. **The origin is the tie.** In turtles, lepidosaurs and crocodylians this is the most proximal of the dorsal division origins, often running past the ectepicondyle onto the shaft; in birds it sits distally near extensor digitorum longus while extensor carpi radialis takes the proximal place — an exact inversion, leaving the two states at exactly opposite probabilities at the nodes flanking Dinosauria. Burch breaks it by function: the avian arrangement serves the automating mechanism of the wing (Vazquez 1994), so he takes the proximal, non-avian position.

occurrences.name: Brachioradialis
occurrences.action: Flexes the elbow; assists pronation and supination toward mid-position.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Upper two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge to the lateral side of the base of the radial styloid process — scored as `radius[distal]`, since the styloid process in this skeleton is the cranial one. **A muscle of the extensor compartment, on the extensor nerve, that flexes the elbow**, which is why this record's confidence is only moderate: it is present in turtles, crocodylians, *Sphenodon* and mammals and absent or uncertain in amphibians, most lepidosaurs and birds, and whether that is one ancestral muscle repeatedly lost or repeated differentiation out of the radial extensor mass is unresolved. Burch's (2014) theropod 'supinator' is scored on this record — read the *Tawa* row beside this one, because the two carry different names for what the synonymy says is the same muscle.

occurrences.name: M. supinator
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Origin only: the fourth of the dorsal depressions on the distal humerus. **Scored on this record rather than on `supinator`, and the corpus now holds the same avian name on two records.** Matsuoka & Hasegawa follow Vanden Berge (1979) in the Nomina Anatomica Avium, and Burch's (2014) Table 1 equates that avian Supinator with Meers's crocodylian 'supinator' and Walker's chelonian 'tractor radii' — which are this record's two existing synonyms, and the basis on which the *Tawa* row was scored here.
