But McKitrick's (1991) loon 'Supinator' sits on the `supinator` record, whose own assessment says the avian usage of the word denotes part of the extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis. **That is a disagreement between sources, not a duplication, and it is flagged rather than resolved**: settling it needs a source that dissects both, which the corpus does not have.

occurrences.name: M. supinator longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Scored on this record rather than on `supinator`, and Russell & Bauer are the source Burch's Table 1 was reading.** He equates the lepidosaur *Supinator longus* with his theropod Supinator, with Meers's crocodylian 'supinator' and with Walker's chelonian 'tractor radii' — the last two are this record's existing synonyms, and the *Tawa* and *Cygnus* rows here follow the same equation. An extensive parallel-fibred belly on the anteromesial forearm arising with the proximalmost part of the extensor carpi radialis from the ectepicondyle by a stout shared tendon; Russell & Bauer read it as a derivative of that muscle and say the two comprise one functional entity. It inserts unipinnately and fleshily along the radial shaft, its distalmost point tendinously on the medial radiale.

occurrences.name: M. supinator (supinator longus)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *epicondylo-radialis*, **Günther's *M. supinator longus*** — which is the lepidosaur name Burch's Table 1 equates with his theropod Supinator, with Meers's crocodylian one and with Walker's chelonian tractor radii, and therefore with this record. From the radial surface of the epicondylus radialis humeri and the elbow capsule to the radial side of the radius as far as its distal end. The *Tawa*, *Cygnus* and *Iguana* rows here rest on the same equation; this is the tuatara end of it.

occurrences.name: Supinator longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Very feebly developed** — a narrow fleshy band from the upper part of the lateral supracondylar ridge ending in a thread-like tendon that passes under the extensor ossis metacarpi pollicis and is inserted mostly into the extensor retinaculum, only slightly into the radial styloid. The contrast with the other two animals is the sharpest on this record: in them the same muscle is larger than a human's.

occurrences.name: Supinator longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **A muscle of great size, relatively much larger than a human's** — from the upper two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge, its tendon running in a groove on the dorsum of the lower radius under the extensor retinaculum to reach the radial carpal, into the outer aspect of which it inserts. It has therefore crossed the wrist, which the thylacine's has not. Macalister records it absent altogether in the Tasmanian devil; Cunningham reports it otherwise near-universal in Marsupialia and enormous in the koala.

occurrences.name: Supinator longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. **A muscle of great size, relatively much larger than a human's** — from the upper two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge, its tendon running in a groove on the dorsum of the lower radius under the extensor retinaculum to reach the radial carpal, into the outer aspect of which it inserts. It has therefore crossed the wrist, which the thylacine's has not. Macalister records it absent altogether in the Tasmanian devil; Cunningham reports it otherwise near-universal in Marsupialia and enormous in the koala.

homology.notes: Present in turtles, crocodylians, Sphenodon and mammals; absent or uncertain in amphibians, most lepidosaurs and birds. Whether this reflects an ancestral muscle with several losses or repeated differentiation from the radial extensor mass is unresolved.

muscles.name: Supinator
synonyms: 'supinator' (Meyers 1996 — avian usage, part of extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis)

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus, the supinator crest of the ulna, and the radial collateral and annular ligaments.
consensus.insertion: Proximal third of the radius, wrapping around its lateral and anterior surfaces.
consensus.action: Supinates the forearm, independently of elbow position.
consensus.innervation: Radial nerve, deep branch — which pierces the muscle and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A stout tendon on the dorsal epicondyle of the humerus, shared with the extensor digitorum communis, lying on the cranial surface of the radius deep to the extensor metacarpi radialis. The bulky belly runs nearly half the length of the radius and inserts by semitendinous fibres on its caudodorsal, dorsal and craniodorsal surfaces — the caudodorsal fibres absent in Gavia immer USNM 504983, a difference between two specimens of one species.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.note: Pelecanoides garnoti UMMZ 225241. McKitrick reports the supinator ABSENT in the diving petrel, in the same dissection series that describes it as a bulky belly in the loon; what is left of its field she treats under the ectepicondylo-ulnaris. Her purpose was to test a proposed loon-tubenose sister relationship, which she does not support — so this row is one of the character differences behind that negative result, not a curiosity. The absence is kept as `no` because her descriptive section states it without qualification, but two other passages soften it and belong here: her character 11 is headed 'reduction or ABSENCE' and reads 'absent OR REDUCED TO AN APONEUROSIS in Pelecanoides', and under the ectepicondylo-ulnaris she allows that 'it is possible that part of this tendinous mass represents all that is left of M. supinator, e.g. the tendinous origin from the dorsal epicondyle in common with M. extensor digitorum communis'. So the belly is gone and the tendon may not be.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.action: Supinates the forearm.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Supinator brevis, from the articular capsule and lateral ligaments of the elbow immediately lateral to the humeral condyle, onto the cranial surface of the proximal two-thirds of the radius. Its origin is capsule and ligament rather than bone.

occurrences.note: Squamates have limited forearm rotation and no unambiguous supinator. Reports of a lepidosaur 'supinator' generally refer to a brachioradialis-like or abductor-pollicis-longus-like muscle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Both supinators: longus from the outer edge of the humerus onto the lower two-thirds of the radius, brevis from the outer condyle along the whole radius. In Gekko the brevis origin is more proximal on the humerus.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.attachmentNote: An insertion surface on the radius.

occurrences.note: Meers (2003) applies the name 'supinator' to what Abdala & Diogo identify as the brachioradialis. This is a naming collision, not a record of the mammalian supinator.
Squamates have limited forearm rotation and no unambiguous supinator. Reports of a lepidosaur 'supinator' generally refer to a brachioradialis-like or abductor-pollicis-longus-like muscle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. The brevis origin sits **more proximally on the humerus** than in Eublepharis.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the entire ventral surface of the ectepicondylus of the humerus, beneath the other antebrachial extensors, with an aponeurosis of origin on its anterior side running almost to the midlength of the belly.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy on the preaxial side of the proximal three-quarters of the radius, a little clear of the elbow joint.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The three genera differ in which stretch of the radius is taken: the proximal three-quarters here, the distal two-thirds in Tachyglossus, the proximal half in the platypus.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the ectepicondylus by two aponeuroses covering the anterior and anteromedial sides of the belly, some fibres arising from the proximal quarter of the medial aponeurosis of origin of the extensor digitorum communis.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy on the anteropreaxial side of the distal two-thirds of the radius, a little clear of the wrist joint.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The only one of the three whose supinator insertion is distal rather than proximal on the radius.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the ectepicondylus, mostly fleshy, aided by an aponeurosis on the anterolateral side.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy on the anteropreaxial side of the proximal half of the radius, a little clear of the elbow joint.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. This record's homology note calls the therian supinator a muscle with no confidently identified counterpart outside Mammalia; the monotreme rows are the outgroup evidence for that statement rather than against it, since monotremes are mammals.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.action: Supinates the forearm, independently of elbow position.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve, which pierces the muscle and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral epicondyle, the supinator crest and fossa of the ulna, and the radial collateral and annular ligaments, to the lateral side of the proximal third of the radius. **This is the only column on this record that is not an argument about a name.** The word 'supinator' is applied by different authors to at least three non-homologous muscles — the crocodylian brachioradialis, part of the avian extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis, and the abductor pollicis longus as 'supinator manus'. The therian supinator, this muscle, has no confidently identified counterpart outside Mammalia, and the human row is what the other three are being mistaken for.

occurrences.name: Supinator brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Feebly developed in all three animals and best marked in this one, where it is inserted into rather less than the upper fifth of the anterior and inner surface of the radial shaft. **Cunningham gives no origin**, so none is scored. Its aponeurotic surface matters elsewhere in this animal: the extensor carpi radialis brevior takes one of its three heads from it.

occurrences.name: Supinator brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Present and feebly developed — the whole of what Cunningham records for this animal. No attachments are scored because he describes none; he gives an insertion only for the cuscus, in which the muscle is best marked.

occurrences.name: Supinator brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Present and feebly developed — the whole of what Cunningham records for this animal. No attachments are scored because he describes none; he gives an insertion only for the cuscus, in which the muscle is best marked.

occurrences.name: Supinator brevis
occurrences.note: Arises just proximal to the anconeus and shares its origin with the extensor digitorum communis, sometimes by a common tendon.
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955). Tendinous from the ectepicondylar prominence; fleshy fibres to the most proximal anconal (dorsal) surface of the radius and to the joint ligaments, fanning distally onto the anterior surface as well. Greatly attenuated distally, where it holds only the anterior surface. Two rows because the insertion covers two faces of one bone.

occurrences.name: Supinator
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. supinator.** This relatively small muscle has a tendinous origin on the proximal cranial face of the dorsal epicondyle of the humerus, just proximal to that of M. extensor digitorum communis. The insertion is fleshy on the proximal radial shaft, extending slightly less than one fifth the length of the bone. No osteological correlates are associated with its origin, but its insertion is on a very clear rugose area on the surface of the radius bounded by intermuscular lines.

homology.notes: Included chiefly as a terminology anchor. 'Supinator' is applied by different authors to at least three non-homologous muscles: the crocodylian brachioradialis (Meers 2003), part of the avian extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis (Meyers 1996), and — as 'supinator manus' — the abductor pollicis longus (Haines 1939; Holmes 1977). The therian supinator as a discrete deep antebrachial muscle has no confidently identified counterpart outside Mammalia.
homology.openQuestion: Is the therian supinator a mammalian differentiation from the deep dorsal antebrachial mass, or does it correspond to one of the reptilian muscles that carry the name?
homology.teaching: The worst single name in the comparative forearm literature. Use it to make the point that a name in a table is a pointer to a description, never a homology claim on its own.

muscles.name: Anconeus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass. Often described as a detached distal part of the triceps field.

consensus.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Olecranon and proximal dorsal ulna.
consensus.action: Extends the elbow; stabilises the ulna during pronation/supination.

occurrences.note: Absent in Ambystoma ordinarium, but Haines (1939) reports it in other urodeles such as Salamandra.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.note: = epicondylo-cubitalis sensu Gaupp (1896).
Absent in Trachemys but present in Testudo, Pelomedusa, Chelodina and Emys.
Absent in Timon but present in at least some lepidosaurs, including Sphenodon.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.note: = anconeus quartus sensu Holmes (1977).

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.action: Assists elbow extension; abducts the ulna in pronation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the caudal area of the last third of the humerus onto the articular capsule and the lateral surface of the olecranon.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus lateralis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the ectepicondylus of the humerus, preaxial to the triceps medialis.
occurrences.insertion: Along the anterior border of the olecranon, descending onto the ulna a little distal to the elbow joint.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. Gambaryan et al. give this as the m. anconeus of Diogo & Abdala (2010) — which is this record — and read it as homologous with the extensor antebrachii ulnaris of lower tetrapods (Haines 1939).

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus lateralis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the ectepicondylus, preaxial to the triceps medialis.
occurrences.insertion: The anterior border of the olecranon, not descending distal to the elbow joint; the insertion is marked by a rugosity.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The shortest insertion of the three, and the only one that leaves a named rugosity.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus lateralis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the ectepicondylus, preaxial to the triceps medialis.
occurrences.insertion: Along the anterior border of the olecranon, descending onto the ulna a little distal to the elbow joint.
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. = m. anconeus sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010). One of the two links in the naming chain that runs the other way: here Gambaryan et al. keep a name of their own for a muscle Diogo & Abdala call by the name this record uses.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.action: Flexes the forearm.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **The insertion is near-certain and the origin is a coin toss — an exact one.** Insertion fleshily on the lateral ulna from just distal to the proximal articular surface for most of its length, at a proportional probability near 1.0 at both bracketing nodes, and *Tawa* has a prominent ridge running from midshaft to the distal end that bounds it and separates it from the abductor pollicis longus origin. Whether the origin shares a tendon with extensor carpi ulnaris sits at exactly 0.50 at the base of Archosauria, and the reason is that every taxon that could break the tie is disqualified: crocodylians lack extensor carpi ulnaris altogether on Burch's reading, anconeus is absent in squamates, in turtles the two are almost entirely fused, and both states are reported for *Sphenodon* (Miner 1925; Haines 1939). Fusion is ancestral for Aves at 0.820. Burch tentatively takes it from the ectepicondyle alongside extensor carpi ulnaris; either way both are the most distal muscles on that epicondyle.

**Burch's crocodylian synonymy conflicts with this record's.** He reads Meers's (2003) 'Flexor ulnaris' as this muscle, and codes extensor carpi ulnaris absent in crocodylians; this dataset's extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris record takes the same name as its own. Both agree the crocodylian muscle is a dorsal-division extensor; they disagree about which extensor. The crocodylian rows here follow Abdala & Diogo (2010) and are left as they stand.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.action: Extends the forearm.
occurrences.innervation: Nerve to anconeus, from the radial nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral epicondyle to the lateral olecranon and the upper quarter of the ulna. Gest gives it its own named branch of the radial nerve, which is the observation that keeps it separate from the triceps in a human — this record's assessment is that the anconeus separates from and refuses to the triceps field readily, varying at species level inside every major clade. The insertion is much shorter than in the outgroups: Burch reconstructs it running most of the length of the ulna in *Tawa* at a probability near 1.0, and here it stops at the proximal quarter.

occurrences.note: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Absent, and the absence is a loss rather than a gap.** Russell & Bauer state the M. anconaeus quartus occurs in *Sphenodon* but has not been reported from any lizard so far studied, and follow Ribbing (1907) and Haines (1939) in reading it as a proximal subdivision of the extensor carpi ulnaris that lizards have lost. Burch (2014) uses the same fact from the other side: with the anconeus absent in squamates, crocodylians lacking extensor carpi ulnaris on his reading, the two fused in turtles and both states reported for *Sphenodon*, the question of whether the two share a tendon of origin sits at exactly 0.50 at the base of Archosauria. This row is one of the four disqualifications that produce that tie.

occurrences.name: M. anconaeus quartus
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, reported by Russell & Bauer (2008). **The first row on a species that has been in `species.json` with none.** Origin in close association with the extensor carpi ulnaris; insertion fleshily along the lateral border of the proximal half of the ulnar shaft.

**This is Russell & Bauer reporting, not dissecting.** They cite Günther (1868), Osawa (1898), Ribbing (1911, 1938), Haines (1939) and Holmes (1977) for the tuatara condition; their own descriptive animal is *Iguana*, which does not have this muscle. The row is scored because the statement is specific and both-ended, and it is flagged here because a reader should know the chain it came down. Holmes reads the muscle as a proximal subdivision of the extensor carpi ulnaris.

**Osawa (1898) describes the same muscle independently and names it the fourth head of the anconaeus** — his muscle 32, *M. anconaeus quartus (richtiger quintus)*, placed in the superficial extensor layer of the forearm beside the extensor carpi ulnaris. That is the same position Haas's and Holmes's readings give it, and it is a second, older, first-hand source for a row that had been carried on Russell & Bauer's report alone.

occurrences.name: Anconeus externus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Cunningham says it can hardly be said to exist**: no muscle of its own, only a few of the lowest fibres of the internal head of the triceps reaching the outer surface of the upper olecranon. Scored present because those fibres are there and he gives their insertion, but with no origin — the origin he describes belongs to the triceps. He notes the muscle varies greatly in development across Marsupialia, and these three animals bracket the range.

occurrences.name: Anconeus externus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Largely developed but inseparably united with the triceps: from the back of the lateral epicondyle to the outer surface of the olecranon and the upper half of the ulnar shaft. That long ulnar reach matters on this animal, because the extensor secundi internodii pollicis arises by two heads and **the anconeus externus runs down the ulna between them**.

occurrences.name: Anconeus externus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Almost identical to the cuscus's but less marked, and it does not extend so far down the ulnar shaft.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955). A tendon from the ectepicondylar prominence of the external humeral condyle carries the fleshy fibres. The belly forms just distal to the humero-ulnar articulation and inserts fleshily on the anterior and anconal (dorsal) faces of the ulna, running out to an attenuated point about halfway along it.

homology.notes: Highly variable at the species level within every major clade — present in some turtles and not others, some lepidosaurs and not others, some urodeles and not others. This intraclade variability is itself the finding: the anconeus separates from and refuses to the triceps field readily.
homology.teaching: A caution against reading a single exemplar species as representative of its clade.

muscles.name: Epitrochleoanconeus
synonyms: part of flexor carpi ulnaris (Walker 1973; Abdala et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle (entepicondyle) of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Olecranon / proximal ulna, medially.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow and stabilises the medial side of the joint; in mammals it forms part of the cubital tunnel roof over the ulnar nerve.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus (anconeus epitrochlearis)
occurrences.note: Galictis cuja: present, and scored from Ercoli et al.'s description. Elsewhere in Mammalia it is inconstant — in humans replaced by Osborne's ligament over the cubital tunnel — but that is a mammal-wide statement and had been sitting in this row as `present: "variable"` alongside scored attachments. Not the muscle a rat or cat dissection guide calls the epitrochlearis: Campbell's rat guide describes that one as a thin medial sheet of the upper arm that EXTENDS the forearm — a latissimus-associated muscle reaching the olecranon — whereas the epitrochleoanconeus runs from the medial epicondyle to the olecranon over the ulnar nerve. The names differ by two letters and the muscles are not the same; no source held here establishes what the lab epitrochlearis is homologous to, so it has no record.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the humerus distal to the caudal opening of the entepicondylar foramen, onto the medial and caudal surfaces of the olecranon, sharing fibres distally with the ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris. The entepicondylar foramen is a carnivoran feature and locates this origin precisely.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus medialis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the entepicondylus of the humerus, close to its tip.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior projection of the olecranon apex.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. = m. epitrochleoanconeus sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010), and homologous with the flexor antebrachii ulnaris of lower tetrapods (Jouffroy et al. 1971). It is separated from the triceps medialis by the nerves converging on the entepicondylar foramen, which is how the two are told apart.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus medialis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the entepicondylus, close to its tip.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior projection of the olecranon apex.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Identical in all three genera, which is worth recording as sameness rather than omitting: three species examined, one arrangement found.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus medialis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the tip of the entepicondylus.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior projection of the olecranon apex.
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus.

occurrences.name: Epitrochleoanconeus
occurrences.action: Flexes the antebrachium.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **The flexor-compartment mirror of anconeus, and like anconeus it is missing from one bracketing clade.** Present only in turtles, lepidosaurs, galloanseriform birds, *Apteryx* and tinamous — not in crocodylians — yet presence reconstructs unequivocally (0.863 at Archosauria, 0.903 at the base of Aves). Part of the reason it looks patchy is that it keeps being absorbed by its neighbour: in *Apteryx* and most turtles it is fused to flexor carpi ulnaris and usually described as that muscle's deep or medial part (Shah & Patel 1964; Walker 1973; Abdala et al. 2008), which is how this dataset's own turtle synonymy has it.

**The origin is a Level II' inference either way** — the derived avian state (origin from the pronator accessorius tendon) is favoured at the base of Aves by 0.527, which is to say not at all. Burch tentatively places it between the flexor carpi ulnaris and pronator accessorius origins on the entepicondyle, the lepidosaur morphology, which may be intermediate between the two states. The insertion is firmer: restricted to the proximal half of the ventral/medial ulna at 0.876 at the base of Aves and 0.698 at the Archosauria + Lepidosauria node, against the long insertion of turtles and *Apteryx* and the distal-half-only insertion of *Sphenodon* and *Tetradactylus*.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed among the 54 upper limb muscles, and scored absent on that basis. **The interest is what it leaves behind**: this muscle bridges the medial epicondyle to the olecranon, and in a human that span is occupied by the cubital tunnel retinaculum, over the ulnar nerve — the same nerve the muscle carries wherever it is present. The record's own consensus action already says the muscle 'forms part of the cubital tunnel roof over the ulnar nerve'. Present in turtles, lepidosaurs, galloanseriform birds, *Apteryx* and tinamous, reconstructed for *Tawa* at 0.863, and repeatedly absorbed into flexor carpi ulnaris where it survives.

occurrences.name: M. epitrochleoanconeus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Tendinous origin from the distal entepicondyle in close association with the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon, its fibres crossing those of the pronator accessorius at about a right angle. Fleshy insertion on the lateral border of the proximal ulna at roughly 45° to the bone's long axis, the belly wrapping around the posterior shaft and so placed to rotate it. **Restricted to the proximal ulna**, which is the state Burch reconstructs for *Tawa* at 0.698 at the archosaur + lepidosaur node against the long insertion of turtles and *Apteryx*.

occurrences.name: Anconeus internus (epitrochleo-anconeus)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Present, with the usual attachments — the back of the medial epicondyle to the inner side of the tip of the olecranon — and supplied by the ulnar nerve, which passes under cover of it to enter the forearm. Its lower border lies against a fibrous cord bridging the hollow between the epicondyle and the olecranon, and that cord gives origin to the flexor carpi ulnaris. **Three marsupials with this muscle present is worth setting against the human row on this record, which is scored absent** — in a human the cubital tunnel is roofed by Osborne's ligament instead. Here the cord and the muscle are in close apposition but not united.

occurrences.name: Anconeus internus (epitrochleo-anconeus)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Present, with the usual attachments — the back of the medial epicondyle to the inner side of the tip of the olecranon — and supplied by the ulnar nerve, which passes under cover of it to enter the forearm. Its lower border lies against a fibrous cord bridging the hollow between the epicondyle and the olecranon, and that cord gives origin to the flexor carpi ulnaris. **Three marsupials with this muscle present is worth setting against the human row on this record, which is scored absent** — in a human the cubital tunnel is roofed by Osborne's ligament instead. In this animal the muscle is firmly united to the upper border of that fibrous cord, so it and the flexor carpi ulnaris are separated by no more than a fibrous raphe.

occurrences.name: Anconeus internus (epitrochleo-anconeus)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Present, with the usual attachments — the back of the medial epicondyle to the inner side of the tip of the olecranon — and supplied by the ulnar nerve, which passes under cover of it to enter the forearm. Its lower border lies against a fibrous cord bridging the hollow between the epicondyle and the olecranon, and that cord gives origin to the flexor carpi ulnaris. **Three marsupials with this muscle present is worth setting against the human row on this record, which is scored absent** — in a human the cubital tunnel is roofed by Osborne's ligament instead. Cunningham reports it generally present through Marsupialia — Galton figures it in the wombat, Gruber in *Dasyurus viverrinus*, Cuvier & Laurillard in the giant kangaroo, Macalister and Young in the koala, Macalister in the Tasmanian devil.

occurrences.name: Entepicondyloulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. entepicondyloulnaris.** M. entepicondyloulnaris and M. pronator profundus are closely associated, and in many places are difficult to distinguish from one another in our CT dataset. The origin is by a common tendon with M. pronator profundus. The entirety of the fleshy belly of M. entepicondyloulnaris lies deep to that of M. pronator superficialis and exists as an extremely thin layer, almost completely fused to M. pronator profundus. The insertion is fleshy on the proximal ventral ulnar shaft, caudal to that of M. brachialis. No osteological correlates were found in the area of insertion. This muscle is notable for being found only in palaeognaths and galloanserans (Hudson and Lanzillotti 1964; Hudson et al. 1972; Vanden Berge and Zweers 1993; Livezey and Zusi 2006; Suzuki et al. 2014; Widrig et al. 2023), and as such is sometimes referred to as the “gallinaceous muscle” in older literature (George and Berger 1966).

homology.notes: Present in all six non-mammalian columns of Table 1. Note the contrast with the anconeus: similar name, opposite mass (ventral vs dorsal) and opposite nerve (ulnar vs radial).
homology.teaching: Pair the anconeus and epitrochleoanconeus explicitly. Near-identical names, opposite sides of the elbow, opposite nerves. A good exam question.

muscles.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
synonyms: part of flexor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris (Diogo & Abdala 2007; Diogo 2007)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus and the proximal ulna.
consensus.insertion: Ulnare/pisiform and metacarpal V.
consensus.action: Flexes and adducts (ulnarly deviates) the wrist.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Part of the flexor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris sensu Diogo & Abdala (2007).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Described as the mirror image of the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis. The four muscles taking the two epicondyles — two flexors medially, two extensors laterally, each pair split proximal and distal — are the clearest instance of the dorsal/ventral mirroring the paper reports for the antebrachium.
occurrences.origin: Distal portion of the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Much of the posterior edge of the ulna, with a slip to the lateral faces of the ulnare and intermedium.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). The most lateral forearm flexor: from the ulnar (medial) epicondyle onto the outer edge of the ulna, the pisiform and adjacent parts of the ulnare. Subdivided into medial and lateral parts in Chelydra, trionychids and Carettochelys, where the lateral part's tendon crosses the palm to fuse with the flexor tendon sheaths — Ogushi (1913) read that part as a separate flexor digitorum communis longus profundus.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Dilkes (2000): present in all major extant reptile groups.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the ulnar condyle of the humerus and the entire laterodorsal border of the ulna onto the pisiform.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Tendinous at the disto-medial humerus, fleshy at 'the ventral manus'. No insertion row: Klinkhamer et al. record that manus insertions were severed during skinning and left deliberately general, so an absent row reads correctly as not recorded, where this row's previous `carpals` asserted a site their wording does not license. Contrast the pronator teres of the same animal, where they do name the ventral CARPALS specifically — that row keeps its carpal insertion.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.action: Flexes and adducts the hand.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Two heads: caput ulnare from the caudal and medial olecranon, caput humerale from the distal humeral entepicondyle. The ulnar head inserts on the lateral surface of the accessory carpal (pisiform) and the wrist fascia, its ligament continuing to the base of metacarpal V.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: Dilkes (2000): present in all major extant reptile groups.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Caput humerale from the apex and postaxial part of the distal border of the entepicondylus, with an inner-side aponeurosis shared with the caput humerale superficiale of the flexor digitorum profundus; caput ulnare from the posterior-postaxial side of the ulna along almost its whole length, excluding the distal end but including the olecranon.
occurrences.insertion: The two heads form a common aponeurosis and a flat tendon running to the proximal apex of the pisiform, from which three pisometacarpal ligaments descend to the bases of metacarpals II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The pisiform is used as a lever exactly as the prepollex is on the other side of the wrist: it lengthens the moment arm for flexion and lateral abduction, and the ligaments carry the pull on to the carpometacarpal II-IV joints.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Caput humerale from the dorsal side of the postaxial distal angle of the entepicondylus, itself divided into two portions of which the posterior fuses with the caput ulnare; caput ulnare from the posterior-postaxial side of the ulna throughout its length.
occurrences.insertion: Both heads onto the pisiform, from which pisometacarpal ligaments descend to metacarpals II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The humeral head is itself split here, its anterior portion staying separate from the ulnar head and its posterior portion fusing with it — a division within a division that neither of the other two genera shows.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.origin: Caput humerale from the apex and postaxial part of the distal border of the entepicondylus, unipennate; caput ulnare tripennate, from the posterior-postaxial surface of the olecranon, descending a little distal to the elbow joint.
occurrences.insertion: A short thick common tendon on the proximal apex of the pisiform. Ligaments from the pisiform to the metacarpals are ABSENT.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The pisometacarpal ligaments both echidnas use to relay the pull onward are missing, which is the same difference the flexor carpi radialis shows on the preaxial side: in the platypus both wrist flexors act on the wrist alone.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.action: Flexes and adducts the wrist.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). Found in every taxon in the study with a consistent morphology; the origin is always the most distal tendon on the entepicondyle, on its posterodistal aspect, and is scored as a single tendon — the multiple lepidosaur parts and the small second avian belly with its novel attachment to the bases of the secondary flight feathers are not the same thing and neither is reconstructed.

**The insertion is equivocal because a bone is not homologous, not because the muscle is unclear.** Crocodylians and most lepidosaurs insert on the pisiform, with a secondary tendon to the ulnare in most turtles and *Varanus*. Birds insert on what is called the ulnare — but the avian element is a de novo ossification and the true tetrapod ulnare disappears during development (Kundrát 2009), so the avian attachment is to a 'pseudoulnare' that is a functional analog and not a homolog. With both primary attachment areas gone the muscle relocated to keep its role. *Tawa* retains a full carpus including an ossified pisiform, so the plesiomorphic pisiform insertion is reconstructed with a possible second attachment to the true ulnare. When the swap happened is unknown: Kundrát reads the ulnare of *Archaeopteryx* as already the avian pseudoulnare.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.action: Flexes the wrist and adducts the hand.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common flexor tendon and an ulnar head from the medial olecranon and the upper two-thirds of the posterior ulna, inserting on the pisiform, the hook of the hamate and the base of the fifth metacarpal. **The pisiform insertion is the plesiomorphic one and humans still have it**, which is not true of either extant archosaur clade: birds lost the pisiform and relocated the muscle to a neomorphic 'pseudoulnare' that is not the tetrapod ulnare at all. The hamate and metacarpal attachments are scored as `distal-carpals` and `metacarpals` rather than as new elements, on the rule that an element here is a homology group and not one species' bone name.

occurrences.name: M. flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Origin only, and **it is on the dorsal side of the humerus** — Matsuoka & Hasegawa group it with the extensor metacarpi radialis, the extensor digitorum communis and the supinator among the four muscles arising from sharp depressions on the dorsal surface of the distal humerus. A muscle named for flexing the wrist, arising from the extensor epicondyle. Elsewhere on this record the origin is the entepicondyle: Burch (2014) makes it the most distal tendon on the entepicondyle in *Tawa*, and the human muscle takes the common flexor tendon from the medial epicondyle. Recorded as the source states it.

occurrences.name: M. flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Tendinous origin from the posterodistal aspect of the dorsal surface of the entepicondyle together with the epitrochleoanconeus, the tendon fanning out on its deep face to give accessory origin for two thirds of the muscle's length. Insertion is chiefly with the **pisiform and the annular ligament**: a broad tendon tapers toward the base of metacarpal V, receives fibres from the extensor carpi ulnaris, and from the ventromesial pisiform and its tendons springs the lateral part of the ventral annular ligament, from which in turn the short flexor of digit V arises. The pisiform insertion is the plesiomorphic state Burch (2014) reconstructs for *Tawa* and that birds lost with the bone itself.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). **Identified but not described.** The muscle is labelled in their figure 2 of the ventral forelimb and appears nowhere in table 3, so the paper records its presence in this animal and states no attachment for it. The row is deliberately left without `attachments`: an empty attachment set reads as unrecorded, where copying Russell & Bauer's entepicondylar origin onto a Freitas row would assert an observation these authors did not publish.

occurrences.name: M. flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. From near the tip of the entepicondyle and the elbow capsule, running along the ulnar border of the forearm to the ulnar side of the ulna as far as its distal end, and to the pisiform. The pisiform insertion is the plesiomorphic one that birds lost with the bone.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The same in all three: a broad thin band arising by two pointed processes, one from the medial epicondyle and one from the olecranon, and taking fibres between them from **a strong fibrous arch bridging the gap between those two bony points** — the arch under which the ulnar nerve enters the forearm. Inserted into the pisiform in every case. The lower border of the anconeus internus lies against the arch without uniting with it.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. The same in all three: a broad thin band arising by two pointed processes, one from the medial epicondyle and one from the olecranon, and taking fibres between them from **a strong fibrous arch bridging the gap between those two bony points** — the arch under which the ulnar nerve enters the forearm. Inserted into the pisiform in every case. As in the thylacine, the anconeus internus lies against the fibrous arch without uniting with it.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The same in all three: a broad thin band arising by two pointed processes, one from the medial epicondyle and one from the olecranon, and taking fibres between them from **a strong fibrous arch bridging the gap between those two bony points** — the arch under which the ulnar nerve enters the forearm. Inserted into the pisiform in every case. Here the arch is inseparably united with the anconeus internus, so that muscle and this one are divided by nothing but a fibrous raphe.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.note: An anterior and a posterior part. The wide tendon of the anterior part is the most palmar and most central of all the tendons attaching to the medial surface of the internal humeral condyle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955). The small deep tendon and the superficial tendon of the anterior part fuse at the proximal end of the os cuneiform, and the combined tendon inserts broadly on its postero-proximal edge. The cuneiform is the avian ulnare.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. flexor carpi ulnaris.** The proximal origin of this muscle abuts the distalmost area of insertion of M. entepicondyloulnaris on the proximal ventral ulnar shaft. The origin of M. flexor digitorum profundus is fleshy, and stretches across approximately the middle two-fourths of the ulna, leaving intermuscular lines on the cranioventral ulnar shaft. At three fourths the length of the ulna it becomes tendinous. The tendon of insertion passes superficially to the belly of M. ulnometacarpalis ventralis and across the wrist cranial to the ulnare. It turns about the pisiform process This is one of the largest antebrachial muscles. It takes a relatively wide origin wrapping around the distal face of the ventral epicondyle (the flexor process), which has a rugose surface. The belly of the muscle runs parallel to the caudal surface of the ulna and is fleshy for most of its length. We did not observe any connections between this muscle and the bases of the secondary remiges in the CT dataset, unlike in the tinamou digitally dissected by Widrig et al. (2023) in which they were clearly visible in the CT data. We observed their presence upon dissecting Fig. 9 Digitally segmented osteology and myology of the coracoid and cranial humerus of Chauna torquata. A: right humerus and coracoid. B: same as A, with Mm. biceps brachii and deltoideus minor added. C: same as B with M. coracobrachialis cranialis added. D: same as C with M. pectoralis thoracica added. Scale bar = 40 mm. K. Widrig et al. 12 the antebrachium and found that they were encased in thick fibrous tissue, which likely prevented the uptake of stain. M. flexor carpi ulnaris inserts via a thick tendon on the muscular process of the proximal ulnare. and that of Mm. propatagialis and extensor longus alulae on either side.

homology.notes: Universal. Ulnar innervation is constant and is the criterion that separates it from the extensor carpi ulnaris despite similar names and adjacent positions.

muscles.name: Flexor carpi radialis
synonyms: pronator superficialis (Sullivan 1962; Shellswell & Wolpert 1977; Meyers 1996; Dilkes 2000)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Bases of metacarpals II and III, or the distal radius/carpals in plesiomorphic taxa.
consensus.action: Flexes and abducts (radially deviates) the wrist.

occurrences.name: Flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. An area of scarring on the face of the radius between the ventral radial crest and the ventral median ridge, read by Bishop (2014) as the insertion — the prominent crest itself carries no scarring. Scored as radius/ventral with no landmark, because the attachment is the surface between two named ridges rather than either of them. Molnar et al. place the separation of this muscle from the humeroantebrachialis at the last common ancestor of crown tetrapods, marked by the appearance of the ventral median ridge.

occurrences.name: Flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Obscured along most of its length by the flexor digitorum communis. Preaxial member of the pair that divides the medial epicondyle between them.
occurrences.origin: Proximal portion of the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior face of the radius, with a slip crossing the wrist to the radiale.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.note: In turtles the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis are usually distinct muscles, though Holmes designated the pronator teres a 'head of the flexor carpi radialis'.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). From the proximal part of the ulnar (medial) epicondyle, passing distally as a narrow band onto part of the radiale-centrale and the first distal carpal. Walker records the insertion of this group ranging from the middle of the radius to the first metacarpal across turtles, and the muscle is **absent in *Trionyx spiniferus***, where he finds a pronator teres and no flexor carpi radialis.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the inner condyle of the humerus, tendinously onto the radiale and muscularly onto the distal radius.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.note: Seems to correspond to the pronator superficialis sensu Sullivan (1962), Shellswell & Wolpert (1977), Meyers (1996) and Dilkes (2000).

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.action: Flexes and abducts the hand.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the middle region of the medial end of the humeral entepicondyle, held by its own retinaculum at the radial carpal, inserting by two loose tendons onto the proximal palmar regions of metacarpals II and III.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: Along the ventral side of the entire distal border of the entepicondylus from its apex to the humeral condyle, interrupted by the origin of the caput humerale profundum of the flexor digitorum profundus; aponeuroses of origin on the inner side shared with the pronator teres and on the outer side with the caput humerale superficiale.
occurrences.insertion: A wide flat tendon to the proximal apex of the prepollex, which articulates with the preaxial carpal complex; from the prepollex the pull is relayed by ligaments to the distal carpals and metacarpals I-III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. **The insertion is on the prepollex**, in all three genera — the element `GAPS.md` §1 singles out as the anuran position-versus-identity case. Monotremes did not lose digit I and have one anyway, and hang more on it than anurans do. The distal ligaments here make it a lever for the carpometacarpal I-III joints as well as for the wrist.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: As in the long-beaked echidna but uninterrupted by the caput humerale profundum, with relatively shorter fibres and more developed aponeuroses of origin, which descend about half the length of the antebrachium.
occurrences.insertion: A flat tendon to the proximal apex of the prepollex, which is connected to the preaxial carpal complex and, by two ligaments, to distal carpals I and II.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Two ligaments to the distal carpals rather than the long-beaked echidna's relay to metacarpals I-III.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.origin: As in Tachyglossidae, but the belly is flattened in the parasagittal plane and more sharply bipennate: the anterior penna bears an aponeurosis facing the humeral condyle and the radius, the posterior penna two, shared with the pronator teres and the caput humerale superficiale.
occurrences.insertion: A round tendon on the proximal apex of the prepollex, with no ligamentous relay onward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The prepollex insertion is shared with both echidnas; what is missing here is the onward ligamentous transfer to the carpals and metacarpals, so the muscle acts on the wrist alone.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.action: Flexes the wrist and abducts the hand.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common flexor tendon to the bases of the second and third metacarpals — the flexor mirror of the extensor carpi radialis rows, reaching the same two bones from the other side of the hand. Note the naming trap this record carries: Sullivan, Dilkes and others call the avian muscle in this position 'pronator superficialis', while Burch's Table 1 gives that same avian name to the pronator teres. The human column is where the two are unambiguously separate muscles with separate nerves.

occurrences.name: M. flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Broadly tendinous origin from the lateral aspect of the humeral entepicondyle shared with the pronator teres, just distal to the coracobrachialis longus insertion, with fibres also arising from the broad tendinous sheet separating it from the flexor digitorum longus for half the length of the antebrachium. It inserts broadly on the ventrolateral aspect of the proximal end of metacarpal I and onto the ventral crest of that bone's head, **where its own insertion tendon then becomes part of the origin of the short flexor of digit I** — the muscle some authors call the adductor pollicis. An insertion that is also an origin.

occurrences.name: M. flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.innervation: N. medianus superficialis and N. humeralis anterior.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *epitrochleo-carpalis radialis*. From the epicondylus ulnaris humeri — the entepicondyle — and the elbow capsule, crossing the forearm obliquely to the distal end of the radius and the wrist capsule as far as the radiale.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Well marked in all three, arising from the medial epicondyle in common with the great flexor mass of the digits. **Its insertion is the variable part**, and Cunningham lists the marsupial range: the second metacarpal in the wombat, phalanger, opossum and bandicoot, the pollical metacarpal in Bennett's kangaroo, the middle metacarpal in the koala. Here the tendon divides in two, to the palmar aspects of the bases of the second and third metacarpals.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Well marked in all three, arising from the medial epicondyle in common with the great flexor mass of the digits. **Its insertion is the variable part**, and Cunningham lists the marsupial range: the second metacarpal in the wombat, phalanger, opossum and bandicoot, the pollical metacarpal in Bennett's kangaroo, the middle metacarpal in the koala. Here it goes partly to the trapezium and partly to the base of the pollical metacarpal — it has not fully crossed onto the metacarpus.

occurrences.name: Flexor carpi radialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Well marked in all three, arising from the medial epicondyle in common with the great flexor mass of the digits. **Its insertion is the variable part**, and Cunningham lists the marsupial range: the second metacarpal in the wombat, phalanger, opossum and bandicoot, the pollical metacarpal in Bennett's kangaroo, the middle metacarpal in the koala. Here it stops on the trapezium alone, the most proximal of the three insertions.

homology.notes: Constant across Tetrapoda. The boundary with the pronator teres is fluid — Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000) treat them as one muscle in several taxa, Abdala & Diogo separate them.

muscles.name: Pronator teres
synonyms: part of flexor carpi radialis (Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000)
pronator profundus (Sullivan 1962; Shellswell & Wolpert 1977; Meyers 1996; Dilkes 2000)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (and the coronoid process of the ulna in mammals).
consensus.insertion: Lateral surface of the radial shaft.
consensus.action: Pronates the forearm; assists elbow flexion.

occurrences.note: Not differentiated in Ambystoma; the urodele forearm lacks a discrete pronator teres.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.note: Ribbing (1907) and Gaupp (1896) disagreed about which anuran muscle this is — flexor antebrachii lateralis superficialis + profundus, or flexor antebrachii medialis.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Arises from the ulnar (medial) epicondyle deep to the origins of flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus, and inserts on the distal end of the radius. Reduced to a single muscle with the flexor carpi radialis in some trionychids.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tendinous at the ventrodistal humerus, fleshy on the ventral carpus. Note the carpal rather than radial insertion — Klinkhamer et al. report it that way for Crocodylus.

occurrences.name: Pronator superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A stout tendon from the tuberculum supracondylare ventrale of the humerus, slightly proximal and partly superficial to the origin of the pronator profundus, inserting by tendinous fibres along the cranioventral surface of the proximal third of the radius. No landmark is asserted for the humeral origin, but not for the reason this note used to give: the 'homology problems with Baumel et al.' remark is made about PELECANOIDES GARNOTI's pronator profundus, where the origin shifts off the tuberculum supracondylare ventrale onto the ventral epicondyle, and in Gavia immer McKitrick names the tuberculum for both pronators without hedging. The row stops at the bone because skeleton.json resolves no tuberculum supracondylare ventrale — and it should not be collapsed onto the entepicondyle, because in this animal McKitrick distinguishes the two: the FLEXOR DIGITORUM SUPERFICIALIS arises from the ventral epicondyle and both pronators from the tuberculum. The tendon of origin fans into an aponeurosis continuous with the humerocarpal band.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.action: Pronates the forearm.
occurrences.note: The median nerve passes between the two heads — a common entrapment site.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the medioproximal and cranial region of the humeral entepicondyle in two bellies, onto the cranial surface of the mediodistal radius.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.origin: A round area on the ventral side of the entepicondylus, plus an aponeurosis on the posterior side of the muscle shared with the flexor carpi radialis.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxial side of the radius distal to its midlength.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. The most superficial muscle on the inner surface of the antebrachium in all three genera.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.origin: A narrower area on the ventral side of the entepicondylus than in the long-beaked echidna, with aponeuroses of origin on both the posterior side — shared with the flexor carpi radialis — and the anterior side of the belly.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxial side of the distal part of the radius.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the apex of the entepicondylus.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal aponeuroses on the anterior and posterior sides of the belly fuse into a flat tendon inserting on the POSTERIOR side of the radius close to its midlength.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Both echidnas insert on the preaxial side of the radius and the platypus on its posterior side, which for a pronator is a change in the line of action and not just in position.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.action: Flexes the forearm and pronates the antebrachium.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). Present in every taxon in the study, with the most proximal origin of all the ventral division muscles. Some neognaths — Charadriiformes, Anatidae — have moved it proximal to the entepicondyle altogether, and that state is slightly favoured at the base of Neognathae (0.528), but paleognaths take it from the entepicondyle itself, which drops the proximal state to 0.082 at the base of Aves and makes the entepicondylar origin unequivocal for theropods. *Tawa* carries the ridge and small anterior projection at the proximal extent of the entepicondyle that probably marks its anteroproximal border.

The insertion is an elongate narrow strip along the anteromedial radial shaft for more than half its length (0.815 at both the Aves and Archosauria nodes), and *Tawa*'s radius has a distinct anteromedial surface defined by ridges running its length. The short proximal insertion of many neognaths is reconstructed as ancestral within that clade (0.677) with, in Burch's words, no clear pattern to its evolution.

occurrences.name: Pronator teres
occurrences.action: Pronates the forearm and assists elbow flexion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common flexor tendon and a deep ulnar head from the medial coronoid process, to the midpoint of the lateral radial shaft. **The insertion has contracted to a point.** In turtles, most lepidosaurs, crocodylians, paleognaths and the reconstruction for *Tawa* it is an elongate strip running more than half the length of the radius, at 0.815 at both the Aves and Archosauria nodes; the human muscle inserts at mid-shaft only. The two-headed origin is shared with the outgroups; the restricted insertion is not.

occurrences.name: M. pronator superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Origin only. Two sharp depressions on the ventral surface of the distal humerus mark the Y-shaped head of this muscle, which is why it is scored `heads` rather than single. The avian name is Pronator superficialis; Burch's (2014) Table 1 equates it with the Pronator teres of crocodylians, lepidosaurs and turtles, which is this record. Note the trap: `flexor-carpi-radialis` in this dataset also carries 'pronator superficialis' as a synonym, from Sullivan and Dilkes, so the one avian name has been used for two muscles.

occurrences.name: M. pronator teres
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Tendinous origin from the lateral entepicondyle in conjunction with the flexor carpi radialis, of which Russell & Bauer treat it as functionally and developmentally a part, following Straus (1942) in deriving it from that muscle. Filiform belly, fibres angled to the radius, inserting fleshily and unipinnately on the anteromesial aspect of the distal half of the radius with some fibres joining the flexor carpi radialis tendon. **Distal half only** — against the elongate insertion over more than half the radius that Burch reconstructs as unequivocal for archosaurs at 0.815.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Broad and thin, broadening again at the insertion, from the caudal epicondyle of the humerus — the entepicondyle, matching the crocodilian origin — to the distal extremity of the radius; their discussion gives the distal third. Freitas et al. present the caudal epicondylar origin as the crocodilian condition and contrast it with *Polychrus*, *Liolaemus*, *Phymaturus* and *Varanus*, where the muscle arises from the distal head of the humerus generally, and with the same lizards' more proximal radial insertions. **Their table also prints an insertion along the caudal margin of the humerus, which is not scored**: a pronator teres cannot insert on the bone it arises from, the discussion names only the radius, and the phrase reads as a table error rather than an observation.

occurrences.name: M. pronator teres
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *epitrochleo-radialis*. With the deep head of the flexor digitorum communis profundus it forms the second layer of the flexor compartment. From the tip of the entepicondyle and the elbow capsule to the ulnar side of the **upper half** of the radius — a proximal insertion, against the elongate one Burch reconstructs as unequivocal for archosaurs and the mid-shaft point of the human muscle.

occurrences.name: Pronator radii teres
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **The coronoid head is absent in all three animals** — a clean contrast with the human row on this record, which carries both the medial epicondyle and the coronoid process of the ulna. Very strongly developed, and its insertion runs almost the whole radial margin of the radial shaft — from the supinator brevis above to the root of the styloid process below.

occurrences.name: Pronator radii teres
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. **The coronoid head is absent in all three animals** — a clean contrast with the human row on this record, which carries both the medial epicondyle and the coronoid process of the ulna. Strongly developed, as in the cuscus.

occurrences.name: Pronator radii teres
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **The coronoid head is absent in all three animals** — a clean contrast with the human row on this record, which carries both the medial epicondyle and the coronoid process of the ulna. Attached only to the middle third of the radius's external border — a much shorter insertion than the cuscus's.

occurrences.name: Pronator superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026). Tendinous origin on the proximal ventral epicondyle of the humerus — the avian ventral epicondyle is the medial (entepicondyle), the flexor-mass origin. **The correlate is named**: the proximalmost of several pits on the ventral epicondyle carries this muscle's tendon of origin. The fleshy belly covers much of the pronator profundus. No insertion row — the passage describing it is broken across the paper's two-column layout and was not read. **M. pronator superficialis.** The tendinous origin of this muscle lies on the proximal ventral epicondyle of the humerus. The proximalmost of several pits found on the ventral epicondyle is associated with this muscle’s tendon of origin. The fleshy belly of this muscle covers much of the surface of M. pronator profundus, and contacts the surface of the ventral ra- mediately expands into a large, fleshy belly as it extends down the length of the dorsocaudal humeral shaft. It is anchored to the proximal portion of the caudal humeral shaft via a stout tendon that also receives fibers from M. latissimus dorsi. This anchoring tendon leaves a prominent circular scar just proximal to the linear scar associated with M. latissimus dorsi. The belly of M. scapulotriceps is in contact with the dorsal portion of M. humerotriceps over much of its length. Distally, it narrows to a tendon and cannot be observed in our CT data distal to the dorsal condyle of the humerus due to the presence of a thick sheath of connective tissue. It inserts in common with M. humerotriceps on the olecranon of the ulna, leaving a faint scar. dial shaft in a small, teardrop-shaped area demarcated entirely by intermuscular lines, as a small tendon.

homology.notes: Present in every column except Caudata. Its absence in urodeles is consistent with the limited forearm rotation of a sprawling, aquatic-ancestral limb; pronation capability increases with the differentiation of this muscle.
homology.teaching: Useful for linking muscle differentiation to a functional capability — forearm rotation — that appears above the urodele node.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the pronator teres, in Rattus and Homo.

muscles.name: Pronator quadratus
synonyms: pronator profundus (Ribbing 1907; Straus 1942; Walthall & Ashley-Ross 2006; Moro & Abdala 2004; Abdala et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Distal ventral (anterior) surface of the ulna.
consensus.insertion: Distal ventral surface of the radius.
consensus.action: Pronates the forearm; binds the distal radioulnar joint.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. pronator profundus. It crosses from the postaxial to the preaxial side of the wrist, which is what makes it a pronator rather than a flexor.
occurrences.origin: Medial side of the ulna, the ulnare and the intermedium.
occurrences.insertion: Radiale and the base of the first metacarpal.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.note: Ribbing (1907) held that Gaupp's (1896) anuran 'abductor pollicis' is in fact the pronator quadratus, not the abductor pollicis brevis.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.note: Probably corresponds to part of Walker's (1973) pronator profundus; the remainder is the pronator accessorius.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: A discrete origin fossa on the ulna — the same proximal-ulnar origin Klinkhamer et al. report for Crocodylus.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy at the proximomedial ulna to the posterodistal radius.

occurrences.name: Pronator profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A unipennate muscle from a stout tendon on the tuberculum supracondylare ventrale, distal and partly deep to the pronator superficialis and proximal and partly deep to the flexor digitorum superficialis, running the whole length of the radius and inserting by fleshy and semitendinous fibres along its ventral surface. The two pronators share one humeral field and are separated by depth and by the level of their tendons, not by different bones — which is why both rows read the same and the difference is in this note.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.action: Pronates the forearm; the prime mover for unresisted pronation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. The deepest muscle of the distal medial forearm: from the medial surface of the distal ulna onto the craniomedial and medial radius, its insertion continuous distally with the palmar radiocarpal and ulnocarpal ligaments.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.action: Pronates the antebrachium and manus.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). Homologous with the avian Ulnimetacarpalis ventralis on Sullivan (1962), which is not obvious from the attachments because the avian muscle has moved its insertion to the base of the carpometacarpus. Origin along a line on the ventral/medial ulna in every taxon studied; the proximal extent is equivocal (elongate at 0.756 at the Archosauria node, reduced-distal at 0.834 in birds), and Burch takes the proximally extensive version covering most of the ulna because *Tawa* is unlikely to have had the derived avian insertion that the distal shift goes with.

**Both insertion rows survive a loss in one bracketing clade.** The carpal insertion is reconstructed at 0.783 at the base of Archosauria and is therefore scored as secondarily lost in modern crocodylians, not absent ancestrally — it is present in some lepidosaurs, all turtles, and, transformed, in birds. The radial insertion is phylogenetically equivocal because birds have dropped it, but its absence there is derived with the wing; Burch's dissections of *Struthio* found a double insertion onto both the distal radius and the carpometacarpus, which does not change the reconstruction's numbers but is the observation that makes the double insertion plausible for *Tawa*.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.action: Pronates the forearm.
occurrences.innervation: Anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial side of the anterior surface of the distal quarter of the ulna to the anterior surface of the distal quarter of the radius. **Distally restricted, like a bird's and unlike a lizard's.** Crocodylians, lepidosaurs and most turtles take the origin from more than half the length of the ulna; birds restrict it to the distal half or less, and so does a human. The carpal insertion present in turtles and some lepidosaurs, reconstructed for *Tawa* at 0.783 and surviving in birds as an attachment to the carpometacarpus, is gone here — the human muscle reaches the radius and stops.

occurrences.name: M. pronator profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Two ulnar origins, no humeral one: the proximal belly by a broad aponeurotic band from the distal posterior fossa of the ulna to about mid-shaft, the distal belly fleshily from the lateral and posterior aspects of the distal third. Both cross the interosseous space obliquely to insert on the posterolateral radius, the distal belly's insertion partly overlain by the proximal belly's. **No carpal insertion**, which is the attachment Burch reconstructs for *Tawa* at 0.783 and reads as secondarily lost in modern crocodylians — Russell & Bauer's *Iguana* does not have it either, though they note it in other lepidosaurs. Macalister (1869) derived the pronator accessorius from this muscle; Straus (1942) put the two in different matrices, this one having invaded the antebrachium by proximal migration from the manus.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Deep, broad and large, its oblique fibres running between the bones of the zeugopodium, broadly from the lateral margin of the ulna to the distal part of the medial face of the radius. Russell & Bauer give the same animal two ulnar bellies and no humeral origin, and take the insertion onto the posterior and lateral radius; the two dissections agree that the muscle is entirely antebrachial and differ on which face of the radius it reaches.

occurrences.name: M. pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *ulno-radialis*, forming the third layer of the forearm flexors. From almost the whole radial side of the ulna, running slightly obliquely distad to the distal half of the radius **and onto the radiale**. That carpal attachment is the one Burch reconstructs for *Tawa* at 0.783 and reads as secondarily lost in modern crocodylians; *Iguana* does not have it and the tuatara does.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Covers the lower fourth of the two forearm bones. Cunningham's verdict on all three animals is that compared with other marsupials this muscle is poorly developed in them.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Covers fully a third of the two forearm bones — more than the thylacine's quarter, though Cunningham still counts all three poorly developed against other marsupials.

occurrences.name: Pronator quadratus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Covers fully a third of the two forearm bones — more than the thylacine's quarter, though Cunningham still counts all three poorly developed against other marsupials.

homology.notes: Present in all six non-mammalian columns and in mammals — unlike the pronator teres, which urodeles lack. The deep pronator is therefore the plesiomorphic member of the pronator group.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the pronator quadratus.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) use 'pronator profundus' as the alternative name for the leg muscle tibialis posterior, which Table 14 pairs with the palmaris profundus 1 or the flexor carpi radialis, not with the pronator quadratus. Whether this record is that muscle needs settling before the edge can be sourced.

Demoted from basis "developmental" to "topological": nothing cited establishes a shared anlage, and CLAUDE.md reserves that value for cases where a source does. Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 pairs the pronator quadratus with the interosseus cruris, and the tibialis posterior ('pronator profundus') with the palmaris profundus 1 in Ambystoma and Timon and with the flexor carpi radialis in Rattus and Homo. This edge crosses those two pairings and conflicts with them.

consensus.origin: Distal ulna, deep to the pronator quadratus.
consensus.insertion: Distal radius and adjacent carpals.
consensus.action: Assists pronation.

occurrences.name: Pronator accessorius
occurrences.action: Flexes and pronates the antebrachium.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Absent in crocodylians, absent in *Sphenodon*, absent in paleognaths except tinamous — and unequivocally present here.** Squamates, turtles and every neognath studied have it, and that distribution reconstructs presence at the archosaur node despite one bracketing clade lacking it entirely. Origin distal to pronator teres at the distal end of the entepicondyle, near the flexor digitorum longus superficialis origin.

**The insertion is where the two nodes disagree and the row is the compromise.** A long insertion over most of the radius is reconstructed at the base of Aves (0.950); a restricted distal insertion at the lepidosaur + archosaur node (0.878). Turtles and some squamates (*Varanus*, *Tetradactylus*) have it distally on less than half the radius, which Russell & Bauer (2008) take as primitive; *Iguana*, *Liolaemus* and a few neognaths put it proximally on less than half. There are no osteological signals on *Tawa*'s radius either way, so Burch splits the difference at the distal end for slightly over half the length. Two rows on one bone, one for the side and one for the level, because the level is the part in dispute.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed, and absent in mammals generally. Its distribution is one of the odder ones on this dataset: absent in crocodylians, *Sphenodon* and paleognaths except tinamous, present in squamates, turtles and every neognath studied, which is enough for Burch (2014) to reconstruct it as unequivocally present in theropods despite one bracketing clade lacking it entirely. Mammals are simply outside that distribution.

occurrences.name: M. pronator profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus GMNH-VA-04-02, Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007). Origin only: one of the three ventral depressions on the distal humerus. Burch's (2014) Table 1 makes the avian Pronator profundus the Pronator accessorius of squamates and turtles, which is this record. **This row disagrees with the *Gallus* row on the same record, which is scored absent.** Burch reports the muscle present in squamates, turtles and every neognath he studied and absent in crocodylians, *Sphenodon* and paleognaths except tinamous, which makes a swan the expected case and a chicken the surprising one. Two species rows disagreeing is what makes the clade roll up as variable, and that is the correct result here rather than something to reconcile.

occurrences.name: M. pronator accessorius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Humeral head from the distal extremity of the entepicondyle, partly fleshy and partly from a superficial aponeurotic band on the elbow joint capsule; a smaller ulnar head from the posterior fossa of the ulna just distal to the olecranon and from the septum against the flexor digitorum longus.
