Both insert together by a common tendinous band on the posterior aspect of the proximal radius. **Proximal radius**, where Burch's reconstruction for *Tawa* had to split the difference between a long avian insertion at 0.950 and a restricted distal one at 0.878 — the lizard is neither, which is part of why that node is hard.

homology.notes: Present only in turtles and lepidosaurs on this sampling. Walker (1973) treated it and the pronator quadratus together as a single 'pronator profundus', so the split is Abdala & Diogo's interpretation rather than a universally accepted division.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum longus / communis
synonyms: flexor digitorum communis longus (Manzano 1996; Manzano et al. 2008b)
flexor primordialis communis + flexor accessorius communis (Ribbing 1907)

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus, with additional heads from the radius and ulna.
consensus.insertion: Palmar surfaces of the phalanges, via a common tendon plate that divides into digital tendons.
consensus.action: Flexes the digits and the wrist; the principal grasping muscle.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum communis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Walthall & Ashley-Ross use flexor digitorum communis; Francis (1934) called the same muscle flexor primordialis communis, the name used for its hindlimb counterpart here. The aponeurosis, not the bone, is the functional insertion — the tendons are its continuation.
occurrences.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Palmar aponeurosis, continuing as four tendons to the proximal end of the distal phalanx of each digit.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: = flexor primordialis communis + flexor accessorius communis sensu Ribbing (1907).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Deep to the palmaris longus, arising from most of the ventral surface of the ulna and joining the same flexor plate, so the two share an insertion and Walker follows Haines (1950) in keeping them separate muscles on that basis. The origin spreads onto neighbouring elements in aquatic groups — a radial head in trionychids, an ulnare head in Dermochelys, ulnare and pisiform heads in cheloniids.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Probably also includes the 'pronator radii teres' sensu McMurrich (1903a) and Holmes (1977), at least in Sphenodon and lizards.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the medial part of the ulnar condyle and the distal two-thirds of the ulna, onto the terminal phalanges of digits I and II.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tendinous at both ends; reaches digit 2 of the manus.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus americana, from Fisher & Goodman's Origin/Insertion paragraphs. M. flexor digitorum profundus: fleshy from the postero-palmar surface of the ulna, from the distal extent of the distal superficial joint ligament out to about one-third of the ulna. Its tendon crosses the wrist beneath the superficial sheath and **hooks around the anterior aspect of the pisiform process of the metacarpus** — the avian carpometacarpus is fused, so the insertion is scored on the metacarpal series with the pisiform process named as the pulley.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis + flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.action: Flexes the digits.
occurrences.innervation: Median nerve; the ulnar half of the profundus by the ulnar nerve.
occurrences.note: The mammalian split into superficial and deep layers with staggered phalangeal insertions is a derived elaboration of a single ancestral flexor plate.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Flexor digitorum profundus, five heads: three humeral (caput humerale laterale, mediale and profundus), one ulnar and one with radial and ulnar origins. The superficialis is not independent — it arises from the surface of the profundus itself and sends three thin tendons to digits II-IV, which is why this record's Theria occurrence lists both.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Probably also includes the 'pronator radii teres' sensu McMurrich (1903a) and Holmes (1977), at least in Sphenodon and lizards.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis + profundus
occurrences.divisionNote: Panthera onca. Seven heads across the two muscles: the superficialis unites an ulnar and a radial head into one belly, which in the jaguar is thick and flattened and divides into four tendons, one per finger; the profundus has five, of which three arise from the humerus completely separately and in one median plane. The SECOND head alone forms the tendon of digit I and the remaining four serve digits II to V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. The radial or deep head of the profundus arises from the distal middle third of the radius and ulna, which is the radius/distal row; the humeral heads take the medial epicondyle. Each tendon runs under the proximal annular ligament, and those of digits II to V continue under the distal annular ligament to insert on the PALMAR side of the distal phalanx. In the jaguar this belly carries TWO SESAMOID BONES — a species-level observation with a skeletal element behind it, and the only one in this paper that a dry specimen could confirm.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.origin: Four heads. Caput humerale superficiale from the ventral side of the distal border of the entepicondylus throughout its length; caput humerale profundum compactly from the ventral side of the spina entepicondyli; caput olecrani and caput ulnare undifferentiated from one another and arising together from the proximal three-quarters of the posterior side of the ulna including the olecranon.
occurrences.insertion: The heads converge on a common tendon which splits, at a palmar sesamoid, into branches to the ventral bases of the ungual phalanges of digits I-V, II-V or II-IV depending on the specimen.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. = m. flexor digitorum longus sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010), which is this record. The variable digital formula is the reduction of the marginal fingers this genus is going through, and it is why the authors recommend Z. bartoni — which keeps all five claws — as the better model. In one specimen a few deep fibres arose from the distal quarter of the posterior radius, which they read as a rudiment of the therian caput radiale.

parts.name: Caput humerale profundum
parts.note: Identified by Gambaryan et al. as the retained ulnocarpalis; see the contrahentium-caput-longum record.

parts.name: Caput radiale
parts.note: A few deep fibres from the posterior radius in one specimen only, read as a rudiment of the therian head.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.origin: As in the long-beaked echidna; the origin of the united caput ulnare et olecrani is outlined on the ulna by two crests.
occurrences.insertion: A large palmar sesamoid is embedded in the common tendon at the point of branching, so that the common tendon inserts on the proximal apex of that bone and five digital branches leave its distal end for the ungual phalanges; the proximal paw pad attaches to its ventral side.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The sesamoid is large enough here that the muscle does not reach the digits directly at all — it ends on a bone in its own tendon, and a second set of tendons continues from that bone. Five digits, against a variable II-V or II-IV in the long-beaked echidna.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.origin: Caput humerale superficiale from the distal border of the entepicondylus — the biggest and, with fibres only about 2 mm long, by far the strongest head; caput humerale profundum with long fibres from the ventral side of the spina entepicondyli; caput olecrani and the smaller caput ulnare from the posterior side of the ulna below the midlength of the bone, here fully separate from one another.
occurrences.insertion: Two palmar sesamoids on the thick common tendon at the level of the carpus. The medial one gives the terminal tendons of digits I-III and the lateral one those of digits IV and V; all five insert on the bases of the ungual phalanges. The thin tendon of the caput humerale profundum inserts on the two sesamoids separately, deeper than the common tendon. Four thick elastin bands run from the sesamoids between the digits into the swimming membrane beyond the claws.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Gambaryan et al. call this muscle a combination of extreme specialisation and profound primitiveness. The specialisation is the caput humerale superficiale: 2 mm fibres give enormous force for underwater rowing and cost the animal finger extension, which is why it knuckle-walks. The primitiveness is the caput humerale profundum, scored on `contrahentium-caput-longum`.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.action: Flexes the digits and the wrist.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). Two parts, one set of insertion tendons. The superficialis is absent in ratites but present in all other birds including tinamous and in crocodylians, so it reconstructs unambiguously; it arises from a single tendon on the entepicondyle sandwiched between flexor carpi ulnaris and pronator teres in nearly every taxon. The second entepicondylar head of some squamates and the ulnar head of a few birds are rare and are not reconstructed (absence at nearly 1.0 at both nodes). The profundus arises from the ventral/medial ulna along most of its length — the full crocodylian and lepidosaur extent, because *Tawa* keeps a four-fingered hand, whereas in birds the origin is curtailed by the proximal extent of pronator quadratus, probably a consequence of digital reduction.

**The digit III slip is the one scored on the hand rather than on the tree.** Slips to the terminal phalanges are plesiomorphic; crocodylians have lost those to their reduced digits IV and V; birds usually retain only the major digit (II), with a digit I slip in tinamous, *Struthio*, *Opisthocomus*, *Balaeniceps*, *Coturnix* and *Bubo* that reconstructs as plesiomorphic at the base of Aves (0.882) — the hoatzin's clawed, tree-climbing chick is the functional reason offered. A digit III slip is present in every outgroup taxon and absent in birds except one *Struthio* specimen, leaving it at 0.043 at the base of Aves, i.e. phylogenetically equivocal; *Tawa*'s well-developed third digit is what puts it back. Digit IV is too reduced and gets none, as in crocodylians.

**A cross-source note on this record's neighbour**: Burch's Table 1 equates the superficialis with Walker's (1973) chelonian 'Palmaris longus', which this dataset holds as a separate, deliberately quoted record whose homology Abdala & Diogo call under-supported. Burch's table is a fourth source identifying the turtle muscle as the humeral head of the long digital flexor rather than as a palmaris longus.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus
occurrences.action: Superficialis flexes the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints; profundus also flexes the distal interphalangeal joints.
occurrences.innervation: Median nerve; the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The two-layer arrangement this record exists to explain, in the animal it is named from.** Superficialis from the common flexor tendon and the middle third of the radius to the shafts of the middle phalanges of digits 2-5; profundus from the ulna and interosseous membrane to the bases of the distal phalanges; and the two insert at different levels on the same digits, the superficialis tendon splitting to let the profundus tendon through. That split-level insertion is the mammalian novelty. In amphibians and reptiles this is a single plate whose tendons end on the terminal phalanges, which is what Burch reconstructs for *Tawa*.

Flexor pollicis longus is scored as a third part: it is the deep flexor to digit I, separated off. **The divided nerve supply is the detail worth keeping** — Gest gives the radial half of profundus to the median nerve and the ulnar half to the ulnar nerve, so one muscle belly spans the boundary between two nerves of the same ventral division.

**Flexor digitorum superficialis** (Gest). Two heads, the humeroulnar from the common flexor tendon and the radial from the middle third of the radius, to the shafts of the middle phalanges of digits 2-5.

**Flexor digitorum profundus** (Gest). Posterior and proximal medial ulna and the interosseous membrane to the bases of the distal phalanges of digits 2-5, its tendons passing through the split superficialis tendons. Its nerve supply is split down the middle — median to the radial half, ulnar to the ulnar half — and the lumbricals arising from these tendons are split the same way, which is a nerve boundary running through one muscle and inherited by another.

**Flexor pollicis longus** (Gest). Anterior radius and interosseous membrane to the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb — the deep flexor plate's radial slip, and the muscle that makes a human thumb able to grip rather than merely oppose.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Three heads — two from the entepicondyle, from the proximal and distal of its two tuberosities, and one from the posterior ulnar shaft sharing a line of origin with the pronator profundus. All three converge on one large flat tendon at the annular ligament, and **the palmar sesamoid is incorporated into its dorsal surface**. Cylindrical tendons arise just proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joints and run midventrally along each digit to the ungual phalanx.

The aponeurosis of this tendon is what other authors call the palmar aponeurosis — see the `palmaris-longus` row for this animal, where Russell & Bauer's conclusion that it has no existence independent of this muscle is recorded.

Iguana iguana, Freitas et al. (2017). Fusiform, the main flexor of the digits, from the caudal epicondyle of the humerus and the lateral margin of the ulna, converging on a broad tendon that divides on the palmar face into five long thin tendons to the bases of the distal phalanges of digits I–V. **The paper contradicts itself about the heads and the contradiction is worth keeping**: the table gives two distinct origins, humeral and ulnar, while the discussion says they did not observe a clear division into radial and ulnar heads in *Iguana* and reads that as a derived condition giving a larger cross-section and a stronger grip. Both origins are scored, since the muscle demonstrably reaches both bones however few bellies it has. Russell & Bauer describe three heads in the same animal, two from the entepicondylar tuberosities and one from the posterior ulnar shaft.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum communis profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *epitrochleo-ulno-digitalis*. Three origins: the superficial and largest from the entepicondyle and elbow capsule; the deep part from the anterior surface of the **ulna and not the radius**, which Osawa states against expectation; and a small accessory head from the volar surface of the ulnare and the base of metacarpal V, joining the main mass from the dorsal side. The whole lies under the ligamentum carpi volare and fans into five slips, one to each digit, **passing through a chiasma tendineum formed for them by the superficial flexor** before reaching the terminal phalanges, where retinacula tendinea fix them to the bone.

occurrences.name: Flexor sublimis, profundus and longus pollicis (amalgamated)
occurrences.innervation: Median and ulnar nerves to the condylar and ulnar portions; the radial portion from the median alone.
occurrences.divisionNote: Cunningham's identification of the three parts is explicitly probabilistic — the condylar portion is 'probably' the sublimis, the radial 'represents' the flexor longus pollicis, the ulnar 'apparently' the profundus — and he gives the reason for the hedge: the nerve supply shows the sublimis and profundus fibres to be thoroughly commingled. Both the ulnar and the median nerve send twigs to the condylar and ulnar portions; the radial portion is supplied by the median alone.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Largely one muscle in all three animals**, arising in three parts: a radial portion from the anterior surface of the radius between the tubercle and the middle of the bone, under the pronator radii teres; an ulnar portion from the olecranon under the anconeus internus and from the posterior border and ulnar surface of the upper half of the shaft; and a condylar portion, intermediate and superficial, from the medial epicondyle. The three unite into a thick mass, and then something unusual happens: **four minute fleshy slips issue from its superficial surface**, each ending in a thread-like tendon, and these four together are the flexor sublimis. The mass gives place to a rope-like tendon grooved along its surface, and the four sublimis bellies and tendons lie in that groove. Below the flexor retinaculum the thick tendon divides into five, one per digit, and the sublimis tendons separate to the four ulnar digits.

occurrences.name: Flexor sublimis, profundus and longus pollicis (amalgamated)
occurrences.divisionNote: Cunningham's identification of the three parts is explicitly probabilistic — the condylar portion is 'probably' the sublimis, the radial 'represents' the flexor longus pollicis, the ulnar 'apparently' the profundus — and he gives the reason for the hedge: the nerve supply shows the sublimis and profundus fibres to be thoroughly commingled. Both the ulnar and the median nerve send twigs to the condylar and ulnar portions; the radial portion is supplied by the median alone.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Arranged as in the cuscus, with two differences Cunningham notes: **the condylar portion is much the largest of the three divisions**, and the ulnar part springs from both forearm bones and the interosseous membrane between them rather than the ulna alone. The four sublimis tendons have no fleshy bellies at all here — they arise directly off the superficial surface of the profundus tendon.

occurrences.name: Flexor sublimis, profundus and longus pollicis (amalgamated)
occurrences.divisionNote: Cunningham's identification of the three parts is explicitly probabilistic — the condylar portion is 'probably' the sublimis, the radial 'represents' the flexor longus pollicis, the ulnar 'apparently' the profundus — and he gives the reason for the hedge: the nerve supply shows the sublimis and profundus fibres to be thoroughly commingled. Both the ulnar and the median nerve send twigs to the condylar and ulnar portions; the radial portion is supplied by the median alone.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. The same three-part origin and the same grooved common tendon as in the cuscus and the thylacine; Cunningham describes the arrangement as very similar across all three and reserves his separate remarks for the thylacine.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Chauna torquata*, Widrig et al. (2026), from diceCT of USNM 666527 with the osteological correlates read off dry skeletons. The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle (lateral) and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle (medial). **M. flexor digitorum profundus.** The origin of M. flexor digitorum profundus is fleshy, and stretches across approximately the middle two-fourths of the ulna, leaving intermuscular lines on the cranioventral ulnar shaft. At three fourths the length of the ulna it becomes tendinous. The tendon of insertion passes superficially to the belly of M. ulnometacarpalis ventralis and across the wrist cranial to the ulnare. It turns about the pisiform process, extends down the length of the cranioventral major metacarpal along with the tendon of M. flexor digitorum superficialis, crosses over the dorsocranial end of phalanx 1 of the major digit, and inserts on the proximal dorsal portion of the second phalanx. No osteological correlates are associated with the insertion. This contradicts Livezey and Zusi (2006), who coded it as inserting on the proximal phalanx of the major digit in Chauna and Anseranas.

homology.notes: The long digital flexor is universal. What varies is the degree of subdivision — a single plate in amphibians and reptiles, two layers with different insertion levels in mammals.
homology.teaching: Good for showing that a mammalian 'novelty' (superficialis/profundus) is a subdivision of something already present, not a new muscle.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexor digitorum longus, and flexor digitorum profundus in mammals.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) give the gastrocnemius no forelimb equivalent in Table 14 — the cell is blank for Timon, Rattus and Homo alike. This edge is not theirs.

consensus.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus.
consensus.insertion: Palmar aponeurosis.
consensus.action: Tenses the palmar aponeurosis; weak wrist flexion.

occurrences.note: Marked '– [but see text]'.

occurrences.name: 'Palmaris longus'
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Small origin on the ulnar (medial) epicondyle, then fanning over most of the ventral forearm in three partially distinct bundles that converge on the **flexor plate**, the tough palmar aponeurosis covering carpus and palm. At the level of the metacarpals that plate splits into five flexor tendons running in fibrous sheaths to the base of each terminal phalanx. With the flexor digitorum longus it is one of only two flexors acting on the terminal segment of a digit. The origin spreads onto the humeral shaft in aquatic turtles, reaching nearly the whole humerus in Dermochelys.

occurrences.note: Absent in Timon, but some lepidosaurs do have a comparable structure.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.note: Galictis cuja: Ercoli et al. describe it present, with a full origin and insertion. The variation they report is in the TENDONS, not the presence — well-defined tendons for digits II/III to IV/V in most specimens, and in one a distal belly differentiating to give a tendon for digit I. Absent in roughly 15% of humans unilaterally or bilaterally, and in many other mammals, but that is a statement about Mammalia and not about this animal; it had been standing in this row as `present: "variable"` while the row also carried scored attachments, which cannot both be true.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the caudomedial margin of the distal humeral entepicondyle onto the palmar fascia, connected indirectly to the radial sesamoid and the accessory carpal. Its insertion is aponeurotic throughout, so it leaves no distal correlate.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.divisionNote: Panthera onca. FIVE tendons, as in the ocelot and against four in Geoffroy's cat. A division count that differs between three species of one family, which is the kind of difference a clade-level row cannot hold at all.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera onca. The palmaris longus lies medial in the forearm and ends by attaching to the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis at the proximal end of the middle phalanx — so its insertion is on another muscle's tendons, not on bone, and the phalangeal row is where those tendons land.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.divisionNote: Leopardus pardalis. Five tendons, as in the jaguar.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leopardus pardalis. The palmaris longus lies medial in the forearm and ends by attaching to the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis at the proximal end of the middle phalanx — so its insertion is on another muscle's tendons, not on bone, and the phalangeal row is where those tendons land.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.divisionNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. FOUR tendons, against five in both the jaguar and the ocelot. Sanchez et al. do not say which digit goes unserved; the parts here are named on the assumption it is the first, which is the usual pattern of loss in the carnivoran manus and is flagged rather than asserted.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leopardus geoffroyi. The palmaris longus lies medial in the forearm and ends by attaching to the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis at the proximal end of the middle phalanx — so its insertion is on another muscle's tendons, not on bone, and the phalangeal row is where those tendons land.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. Absent, and Gambaryan et al. list the absence among the primitive features of monotremes as a whole. What stands in its place is a bundle of the cutaneus trunci running down the flexor side of the antebrachium to the wrist and joining, through the fascia palmaris manus, the preaxial side of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus near its branching point — which they call the apparent predecessor of the therian palmaris longus. A skin muscle occupying the position of a limb muscle that does not yet exist.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Absent, and without even the cutaneus trunci bundle the long-beaked echidna has in its place.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Absent. Here the cutaneus trunci runs to the EXTENSOR side of the antebrachium instead, terminating at the wrist in a subcutaneous aponeurosis that splits into four interdigital branches, each bifurcating to insert on opposing sides of the claws of adjacent digits.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.action: Tenses the palmar aponeurosis; weak wrist flexion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common flexor tendon to the palmar aponeurosis. **This record is quoted because its deep homology is not established, and the human muscle is the referent, not the evidence.** Abdala & Diogo name the 'palmaris longus' and the 'rhomboideus' as the two structures whose correspondence with the mammalian muscles of those names is explicitly under-supported, and ask for innervation and development across a broader amphibian and reptilian sample. Burch's (2014) Table 1 answers from a fourth direction, equating Walker's chelonian 'palmaris longus' with the humeral head of flexor digitorum longus instead. Gest also lists a palmaris brevis, a dermal muscle of the hypothenar skin with no counterpart anywhere else in this dataset; it is not scored.

occurrences.note:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Scored absent, and the reason bears directly on this record's open question.** Russell & Bauer address the tendinous mass in the lizard palm that authors have called the palmar aponeurosis and conclude it is not a sheet of fibrous material giving origin to muscle fibres but **the common tendon of the M. flexor digitorum longus**, with no existence independent of the ventral antebrachial muscles. Haines (1950) had derived it from the thin fascia superficial to the long flexor tendons. So there is no 'palmaris longus' muscle here to score, and the structure the name points at belongs to another record.

This is the third source in the corpus to say something of that shape. Abdala & Diogo name the 'palmaris longus' and the 'rhomboideus' as the two structures whose homology with the mammalian muscles of those names is explicitly under-supported, and ask for exactly the innervation and development work across amphibians and reptiles that Russell & Bauer also call for; Burch's (2014) Table 1 equates Walker's chelonian 'palmaris longus' with the humeral head of flexor digitorum longus. Three independent readings, all pointing away from the mammalian muscle.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Almost no direct attachment to the medial epicondyle** — it springs instead from the superficial surface of the great digital flexor — and its powerful tendon drives into the middle of the palmar pad, where it breaks into four strong slips joining the flexor sheaths of the four ulnar digits. So it ends on tendon, not on fascia.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Arranged as in the thylacine — arising largely off the great digital flexor rather than the epicondyle — but in the palm it spreads out into a distinct palmar fascia instead of ending in four slips.

occurrences.name: Palmaris longus

parts.name: Slip common with the digital flexor
Deep slip from the digital flexor

occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Three small slips rather than one muscle**: a very delicate fasciculus straight off the medial epicondyle; a larger slip arising in common with the great digital flexor; and a deeper portion issuing from that flexor's superficial surface. All three join the palmar fascia. Two of the three heads therefore take origin from another muscle.

homology.notes: Quoted deliberately. Abdala & Diogo list this as one of the two structures (with the 'rhomboideus') whose homology with the mammalian muscle of the same name is explicitly under-supported. Their stated requirement: a detailed analysis of the innervation and development of the 'rhomboideus' and 'palmaris longus' across a broader sample of amphibian and reptilian taxa. Burch's (2014) Table 1 answers the question from a fourth direction: he equates Walker's (1973) chelonian 'Palmaris longus' with the humeral head of flexor digitorum longus (his Flexor digitorum longus superficialis), alongside Meers's crocodylian 'Flexor digitorum longus pars humeralis' and the avian 'Flexor digitorum longus superficialis'. On that reading the turtle muscle is not a palmaris longus at all but the superficial head of the long digital flexor, which is the second of the two options this record's open question poses.
homology.openQuestion: Is the turtle 'palmaris longus' homologous with the mammalian palmaris longus, or an independently differentiated superficial flexor?
homology.teaching: An honest example of a named, textbook-familiar muscle whose deep homology is not actually established.

consensus.origin: Distal ulna.
consensus.insertion: Carpus, giving rise to the contrahentes digitorum.
consensus.action: Flexes and adducts the digits toward the axis of the hand.

occurrences.name: Contrahentium caput longum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Its insertion tendon is itself the origin of the contrahentes digitorum, so the two form a chain from the zeugopod to the phalanges.
occurrences.origin: Internal surface of the ulna and the fascia connecting radius and ulna.
occurrences.insertion: An extensive tendon connecting the carpal bones.

occurrences.name: Contrahentium caput longum
occurrences.note: Attachment rows for this taxon describe the foot and have been moved to the pes record.
Abdala & Diogo report that a few lizards may have a small muscle somewhat resembling the contrahentium caput longum of Ambystoma.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus, caput humerale profundum
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the spina entepicondyli — the distal styloid process of the entepicondylus of the humerus — by long fibres, the belly then squeezing down between the caput olecrani and the caput ulnare of the flexor digitorum profundus.
occurrences.insertion: A thin terminal tendon running to the manus in a groove on the deep side of the common flexor tendon, inserting separately on the two palmar sesamoids and, through the ligamentum flexorium commune transversum, on the ventral side of the ulnare.
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **This record says the muscle was lost in amniotes; Gambaryan et al. say it was not.** Straus (1942) held the urodele ulnocarpalis to have dissolved into the flexor digitorum profundus beyond amphibians. Their evidence that it kept its identity instead is topological and ligamentous, not merely positional: the head wedges between the caput olecrani and the caput ulnare exactly as the urodele ulnocarpalis wedges between the two heads of the palmaris communis profundus sensu Miner (1925) — which are the flexor accessorius lateralis and flexor accessorius medialis of Diogo & Abdala (2010), both records in this dataset — and it ends on the ligamentum flexorium commune transversum, which they identify as the surviving postaxial segment of the transverse subcarpal ligament that the urodele muscle specifically inserts on. On their reading the muscle is not lost but captured: its origin has migrated from the ulna onto the humerus and it has been imprisoned inside the former palmaris communis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The origin is on the HUMERUS, against this record's consensus origin on the distal ulna, and that migration is the substance of the claim rather than an inconvenience for it.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus, caput humerale profundum
occurrences.origin: Ventral side of the spina entepicondyli of the humerus, the belly hidden in the cleft between the caput humerale superficiale and the caput ulnare et olecrani.
occurrences.insertion: A thin tendon running separately beneath the main flexor tendon almost as far as the palmar sesamoid.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. `uncertain` rather than `yes` because the head itself is present but the structure that carries Gambaryan et al.'s identification is not confirmed in it. They rest the argument on the ligamentum flexorium commune transversum, which they find in the platypus and report from this animal only on Kajava's (1911) authority and, they say, probably as individual variation. Straus (1942) reports it in some lipotyphlan insectivores as well, so if the identification holds the muscle is not a monotreme relic either.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum profundus, caput humerale profundum
occurrences.origin: Compact origin on the ventral side of the spina entepicondyli of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: A thin terminal tendon running separately under the common tendon of the other heads, coated on its inner side by the distal-most fibres of the caput ulnare, and fusing into the deep side of that common tendon at the level of the wrist.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. `uncertain` on the same grounds as the short-beaked echidna: the head is described in full and is the most distinct of the four, but the transverse ligament that makes it identifiable as the ulnocarpalis is reported only in the platypus. Three rows on one record disagreeing about a muscle's identity rather than its presence is what this field is for.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The ulnocarpalis is present in urodeles and monotremes and gone in a human hand; Gambaryan et al. (2015) argue it survives in *Ornithorhynchus* against the transverse subcarpal ligament, and Straus (1942) reported that ligament in some lipotyphlan insectivores. Neither muscle nor ligament is in a human, which is why this record's therian rows are thin.

homology.notes: An amphibian muscle lost in amniotes, retaining only its distal derivatives (the contrahentes digitorum). One of the clearest cases of plesiomorphic retention in Lissamphibia.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the contrahentium caput longum, in Ambystoma.

muscles.name: Flexor accessorius lateralis
synonyms: caput dorsale of flexor palmaris profundus (Straus 1942)
palmaris profundus (Gaupp 1896; Straus 1942; Manzano et al. 2008b)

consensus.origin: Ulna and/or radius, deep in the antebrachium.
consensus.insertion: Deep palmar flexor tendons.
consensus.action: Assists digital flexion.

occurrences.name: Flexor accessorius lateralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibres run diagonally toward the radius and first digit. Inserting on the deep face of an aponeurosis is what lets it tension the palm rather than move a bone.
occurrences.origin: Distal end of the ulna, the ulnare and the intermedium.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal surface of the palmar fascia.

occurrences.note: Absent as an independent muscle in extant amniotes.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed for the hand. **The foot kept it**: the human quadratus plantae is the surviving flexor accessorius of the pes, and is scored on `flexor-accessorius-lateralis-pes`. A muscle present in one limb and absent in the serially corresponding position of the other, in the same animal — which is a caution about serial correspondence rather than evidence for it.

homology.notes: Lissamphibian retention; absent as an independent muscle throughout extant Amniota.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexor accessorius lateralis, in Ambystoma.

muscles.name: Flexor accessorius medialis
synonyms: caput volare of flexor palmaris profundus (Straus 1942)

consensus.origin: Ulna, deep in the antebrachium.
consensus.insertion: Deep palmar flexor tendons.
consensus.action: Assists digital flexion.

occurrences.name: Flexor accessorius medialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Distinguished from the lateral accessory only by a more extensive origin — the two are otherwise parallel-fibred straps with the same insertion.
occurrences.origin: Approximately the distal third of the ulna, the ulnare and the intermedium.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the palmar fascia.

occurrences.note: Absent as an independent muscle in extant amniotes.
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed; see [[flexor-accessorius-lateralis]] for the hand-versus-foot contrast.

homology.notes: Present only in urodeles among the sampled taxa — the most restricted distribution in the forearm table.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexor accessorius medialis, in Ambystoma.

muscles.name: Flexores breves superficiales
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the manus.
synonyms: flexores digiti brevis superficiales (Abdala et al. 2008)

consensus.origin: Palmar aponeurosis and carpal region.
consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges.
consensus.action: Flexes the digits at the metacarpophalangeal joints.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Slips lie on both sides of the metacarpals of digits II and III, but only on the medial side for digits I and IV — an asymmetry across the hand that tracks the axis of the manus.
occurrences.origin: Dorsal surface of the palmar fascia.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral edges of the distal ends of the metacarpals.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Arises from the ventral surface of the flexor plate — **a muscle whose whole origin is another muscle's insertion**, which is why the plate is only visible at its proximal border in a superficial dissection. It breaks into eight slips with the flexor tendons emerging between them, onto the sides of the proximal phalanx of each digit and the flexor tendon sheaths: two slips to each of the middle three digits, one each to the first and fifth. Ribbing (1938) treats it as five distinct muscles; Walker keeps it single because in turtles the parts separate only at their insertions.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Flexor digitorum brevis, from the ulnare onto the terminal phalanx. In Gekko the insertion is distally on the antepenultimate phalanx.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.note: Includes part of the flexores breves sublimes sensu Holmes (1977) and probably the flexor digiti quinti and/or transversus palmaris sensu Meers (2003).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Meers's crocodylian names are bridged to this record through Abdala & Diogo's Table 1, which gives the Caiman column with explicit 'sensu Meers, 2003' equivalences. = Mm. flexor digitorum brevis superficialis I-IV. A complex of small bipinnate bellies from the distal carpal row and tendinously from the overlying flexor digitorum longus, extending to the pisiform, each inserting by a discrete tendon onto the sides of one or more phalanges. Their tendons split at about mid-metacarpal to let the flexor digitorum longus tendons through. **Digit V appeared to lack such a muscle** in the specimens examined.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Inserts distally on the **antepenultimate** phalanx rather than the terminal one.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.origin: Four preaxial flexors for digits I-IV and sometimes up to three postaxial ones for digits II-IV. The first arises from the preaxial edge of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus and the rest from its ventral side, the origin spreading proximally onto the fascia palmaris manus and even the fascia antebrachii.
occurrences.insertion: The preaxial flexors pass preaxial to the corresponding digital tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus and insert through the metacarpophalangeal subarticular ligament on the preaxial base of phalanx 1; where a postaxial flexor is also present the two embrace the profundus tendon like the perforated tendon of the therian flexor digitorum superficialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. **These bellies are inside the hand**, not the forearm, and Gambaryan et al. count that among the primitive monotreme features while arguing the series is the therian flexor digitorum superficialis — on the strength of the embracing insertion, and of the same distal origin turning up in tupaias (Panyutina et al. 2015) and felids (Haines 1950). In other therians the muscle has migrated proximally onto the profundus aponeurosis or onto the entepicondylus itself.

parts.name: Postaxial flexores breves superficiales II-IV
parts.note: Most often present in digit IV, more rarely in II and III.

occurrences.divisionNote: The set varies between specimens of this genus, which the authors tie to the reduction of the marginal fingers.

occurrences.name: Flexor brevis superficialis I
occurrences.origin: The preaxial edge and adjacent dorsal side of the palmar sesamoid of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxially at the end of the preungual phalanx of the thumb.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. **One muscle, for digit I alone**, against four or more in the long-beaked echidna and four in the platypus — the most reduced condition of the three by a wide margin. Gambaryan et al. note it could alternatively be read as the lumbricalis I, and reject that on the general grounds that no tetrapod supplies the thumb from the lumbrical series.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.origin: Four muscles for digits I-IV, from the ventral side of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus at the proximal border of its sesamoids.
occurrences.insertion: The terminal tendons thin into sheets which disappear distally into the loose elastic tissue enveloping each digit. In digit I the tendon is distinct as far as the metacarpophalangeal subarticular ligament; in digits II-IV the tendons reach the midlength of the first phalanges, where they embrace the corresponding profundus tendons as very thin perforated tendons.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Gambaryan et al. correct Diogo & Abdala (2010) here: the tendons embrace the profundus tendons but are NOT fused with them, which matters because the embracing-not-fusing relation is what the flexor digitorum superficialis homology rests on.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.action: Flexes the metacarpophalangeal joints.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). **Burch reconstructs this origin against his own plesiomorphy argument, and says so.** In lepidosaurs and turtles these bellies arise entirely from the annular ligament covering the carpals; that ligament is absent in extant birds and crocodylians, both of which have modified wrists. *Tawa*'s wrist is closer to a lepidosaur's than to either, so the ligament was probably retained and these muscles probably arose from it — which would make the shift to a distal-carpal origin a later consequence of theropod wrist modification. Burch nonetheless scores the distal-carpal origin, on the possibility that it is an archosaurian synapomorphy already present here. The carpal row is that choice; the flexor-tendon row is the crocodylian condition, where the muscle arises from the distal carpals and the flexor digitorum longus tendon together, and matches the avian Flexor alulae from the base of the carpometacarpus and the same tendon.

The distal tendons bifurcate to let the long flexor tendons pass and then insert on either side of the flexor processes — phalanx 1 of digits I and II, phalanx 2 of digit III. Digit I is the exception: no bifid tendon in lepidosaurs or birds, a simple insertion on the ventromedial base of phalanx 1, favoured at the base of Archosauria at 0.786.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Scored uncertain rather than absent, and the uncertainty is about which record the human muscles belong to, not about what is there. The superficial short flexor layer has no muscle in the human hand that is unambiguously its own: the candidates — palmaris brevis, the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis — are assigned to this layer by some authors and to the deep layer by others, and the deep layer's members are scored on `flexores-breves-profundi`. Compare the foot, where flexor digitorum brevis is the surviving superficial layer and is scored plainly. The hand lost the layer or absorbed it; the sources do not agree which.

occurrences.name: Mm. flexores digitores breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **The whole complex arises from the annular ligament**, with contributions laterally from the fascia of the flexor carpi ulnaris — not from the distal carpals. That is the arrangement Burch (2014) argues *Tawa* probably had, since its wrist was more lepidosaur-like than either extant archosaur's, before deciding to score the distal-carpal origin anyway on the possibility that it is an archosaurian synapomorphy; this row is the alternative he was weighing. Insertions are on the ventral tongues of the phalanges, with the tendon to each of digits II, IV and V splitting around the long flexor tendon and rejoining dorsal to it; digit III has no perforated short flexor tendon, and the slip to digit I is undivided and inserts on the mesial margin of the first phalanx.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum communis sublimis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. The superficial layer of the palm, and **its whole function is to be perforated**: it overlies the deep flexor and forms a *chiasma tendineum* through which the deep tendons pass to reach the terminal phalanges. The same bifurcating arrangement Russell & Bauer describe for *Iguana* and Burch reconstructs for *Tawa*, and the same relationship the human flexor digitorum superficialis has with the profundus — one of the clearest topological constants in the dataset.

homology.notes: Present in all six non-mammalian columns. Part of the three-layer intrinsic palmar system (superficiales, contrahentes, profundi) that mammals largely reduce.
homology.teaching: Introduce the three intrinsic layers together — superficiales, contrahentes, profundi — then show what mammals kept.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 15 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexores breves superficiales.

muscles.name: Contrahentes digitorum
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the manus.
synonyms: part of flexores digitorum breves medii (McMurrich 1903a,b; Lewis 1989)

consensus.origin: Carpus and the palmar aponeurosis, along the axis of the hand.
consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges, drawing the digits toward the hand's axis.
consensus.action: Adducts the digits toward the axial digit.

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Lies deep to the insertion tendons of the flexores breves superficiales. Part of its origin is tendinous rather than skeletal, on the contrahentium caput longum tendon.
occurrences.origin: The insertion tendon of the contrahentium caput longum, and the carpals.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal end of the proximal phalanx of each digit.

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.note: Probably includes the adductor pollicis sensu Manzano et al. (2008b).
occurrences.attachmentNote: The contrahens indicis arises by tendon from the mediodistal distal carpal 3-4-5 and inserts on the lateropalmar surface of the basal phalanx of digit II; the contrahens digiti V arises lateral to it. A separate contrahens serves the prepollex.

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.note: Includes the adductor digiti minimi sensu Walker (1973).

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.note: Include the flexor digitorum V transversus I and II of Abdala & Moro (2006).

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Meers's crocodylian names are bridged to this record through Abdala & Diogo's Table 1, which gives the Caiman column with explicit 'sensu Meers, 2003' equivalences. = Mm. flexores digitorum intermedii, the layer between the superficial and deep palmar musculature. The digit IV/V belly arises from the distal margin of the ulnare and lies in the plane of the lumbricals, usually inserting on the distal end of P1 of digit IV with a frequent accessory tendon to the distal metacarpal of digit V. The digit V belly arises from the distal carpal proximal to digit V and inserts on the ventral base of its P1. **Both are inconsistent** — Meers found the digit V belly commonly but not always, even within Alligator mississippiensis.

occurrences.name: Adductor pollicis (+ palmar interossei)
occurrences.note: Rattus norvegicus, from Abdala & Diogo's Tables 2-3. The mammalian adductor pollicis is generally regarded as a surviving contrahens; the rest of the layer is lost.

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.note: Tawa hallae. Scored uncertain, and the uncertainty is about presence rather than about attachments. Burch (2014) groups the muscles variously called Flexor digitorum brevis intermedius or Contrahentes digitorum as an assortment of smaller muscles related to the short flexors that vary between and sometimes within clades, typically arising on the medial carpus and inserting on the fourth and/or fifth digits, and declines to reconstruct them: highly speculative in extinct taxa. **He goes further and gives a reason to expect their absence** — lizards showing the same pattern of reduction of digits four and five have lost them (Berger-Dell'Mour 1983), and *Tawa*'s digit IV is highly reduced. A muscle group whose insertions are on the digits this animal was in the process of losing.

occurrences.name: Adductor pollicis
occurrences.action: Adducts the thumb.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Oblique head from the capitate and the bases of the second and third metacarpals, transverse head from the shaft of the third, both to the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. **One contrahens survives in a human and this is it.** The contrahens layer runs a muscle to every digit in a lizard or a crocodylian; humans have lost all of them except the one to digit I, which is why the adductor pollicis has no partner and looks like a thenar muscle rather than a member of a series. Compare the *Tawa* row on this record, scored uncertain because Burch expects the same layer to have been lost there for the same kind of reason — reduction of the lateral digits.

occurrences.note: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Scored uncertain rather than absent. Russell & Bauer do not recognise a contrahens layer in the lizard manus as such; where Haines (1950) listed Mm. contrahentes for *Varanus*, they map that stratum onto two things they do recognise — the abductor of the fifth metacarpal and the interosseus ventralis of digit I — and warn that their synonymies of Haines's terms are tenuous and may not correspond exactly, because exact correspondence cannot be arrived at on the available evidence. That is a stated inability to decide, which is what `uncertain` is for. Both muscles they map it onto are scored: see [[abductor-digiti-minimi]] and [[flexores-breves-profundi]].

occurrences.name: Palmar group (four adductors)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. **Four adductors, arranged to antagonise the abductors one for one**: all arise close together from the palmar carpus and radiate to their insertions — the first to the ulnar side of the first phalanx of the thumb, and so the representative of the human adductor pollicis; the second to the ulnar side of the index; the third to the radial side of the ring finger; the fourth to the radial side of the little finger. Cunningham's point is the symmetry: the two marginal abductors and the first and fourth dorsal interossei each have a dedicated antagonist, while the second and third dorsal interossei act as adductor and abductor of the middle finger by turns, as in a human hand.

occurrences.name: Palmar group (three adductors)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Three well-marked muscles lying on the intermediate group — a large adductor of the little finger, an adductor of the ring finger and an adductor of the index — with the same insertions as the phascogale's. They arise from the front of the carpus, those of the ring finger and index by a common tendon partly under the origin of the adductor minimi digiti. **The adductor of the thumb is normally fused with the ulnar portion of the flexor brevis pollicis**, but in one of Cunningham's four dissections of this hand it came away as a distinct slender slip with the phascogale's attachments — which is why it is scored here as a variable part rather than as absent.

occurrences.name: Palmar group (four adductors and a raphe)

parts.name: Transverse fasciculus to the index and annularis

occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus, and the most instructive of the three. In a human the adductor pollicis seeks the middle line of the hand for its origin, taking the third metacarpal so it can draw the thumb across the palm; in the thylacine and the phascogale Cunningham sees a tendency towards the same thing. **In the cuscus every adductor has got there, but by a different route: a median fibrous raphe runs down from the base of the third metacarpal, and the adductors arise from either side of it** — pollicis and minimi digiti opposite each other on its upper two-thirds, and also by a few fibres from the front of the carpus; the small adductors of index and ring finger opposite each other below them. A separate fleshy fasciculus lies in front of the raphe, connected to it in no way, passing round the base of the middle finger to attach at one end to the adductor tendon of the ring finger and at the other to that of the index — an adductor of both which, having no intermediate attachment, must act on both at once. Together with the raphe these muscles form a thin stratum hiding most of the intermediate group.

occurrences.name: Adductor minimi digiti
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, **manus**, and Cunningham dissected it to check a sentence of Meckel's — that in the platypus the interossei of the hand behave exactly like those of the foot, only thinner and more slender. He found the arrangement very different. In the hand the whole plantar layer is reduced to **a single minute thread-like muscle, the adductor minimi digiti**, where the foot has four well-marked adductors. The dorsal interossei are absent too, though strands of tough fibrous tissue in the intermetacarpal spaces may represent them. Only the intermediate layer holds up: a two-slipped flexor brevis for each digit except the minimus, which has an ulnar head alone.

homology.notes: Present across all non-mammalian columns; reduced to the adductor pollicis (and possibly some palmar interossei) in mammals. This layer is a large part of why lizard and salamander hands have more intrinsic muscles than human hands.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 15 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the contrahentes digitorum.

muscles.name: Flexores breves profundi
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deepest ventral intrinsic layer of the manus.
synonyms: flexores digitorum breves profundi (McMurrich 1903a,b; Ribbing 1938; Holmes 1977)

consensus.origin: Metacarpals, deep in the palm.
consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges and the sesamoids at the metacarpophalangeal joints.
consensus.action: Flexes the metacarpophalangeal joints; with the intermetacarpales, controls digit spread.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves profundi
occurrences.attachmentNote: The deepest of the short flexor layers.
occurrences.origin: Carpals at the bases of their respective digits.
occurrences.insertion: Chiefly the metacarpal, and also the proximal end of the proximal phalanx, of each digit.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves profundi
occurrences.attachmentNote: The medial flexor indicis brevis profundus arises by tendon from the medial distal carpal 3-4-5 and inserts fleshily on the mediopalmar metacarpal II and on the ligament connecting the prepollex.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves profundi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Meers's crocodylian names are bridged to this record through Abdala & Diogo's Table 1, which gives the Caiman column with explicit 'sensu Meers, 2003' equivalences. = M. flexor digitorum profundus digiti I-V, and possibly also the flexor digitorum intermedius of digit V. From the ventral surface of the distal carpal row, extending slightly onto the metacarpal base, by a flat broad tendon onto the flexor process at the base of the first phalanx. In some Alligator the digit I tendon is irregularly divided in two.

occurrences.name: Interossei (palmar and dorsal)
occurrences.note: The mammalian interossei are generally derived from the flexores breves profundi together with the intermetacarpales.
occurrences.action: Abduct and adduct the digits; flex the metacarpophalangeal joints.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Ten fleshy bellies, a medial and a lateral for each digit, arising at the proximal area of the corresponding metacarpal. The pair for digit III and the lateral belly for digit II arise from the plantar process of carpal III; the digit I bellies from metacarpal I, carpal I and marginally the radial sesamoid.

occurrences.name: Interossei
occurrences.origin: Interossei I-III from the prepollex; interossei IV and V from the pisiform and from the ligament connecting it to metacarpal IV.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxially (mediales) or postaxially (laterales) on the metacarpophalangeal joints, though reduction of the marginal digits displaces the insertions of interossei I and V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. = mm. flexores breves profundi sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010), which is this record. The set is variable: interossei I and II mediales and II and V laterales are the commonest, and all six others are possible. Special names apply at the margins — interosseus I medialis is the opponens pollicis, I lateralis the adductor pollicis, V lateralis the opponens digiti quinti.
occurrences.divisionNote: Of the ten possible muscles the authors found no fixed set in this genus, which is the individual variation below the elbow the paper is careful to document rather than average away.

occurrences.name: Interossei
occurrences.origin: The muscles of digits I and II from the prepollex — three by a common tendon from its distal end, the interosseus II lateralis fleshy; those of digit III from the ligament between the prepollex and metacarpal III; the occasional interosseus IV medialis from the pisiform.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxially or postaxially on the metacarpophalangeal joints of the digits they serve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Five muscles always present — interosseus I medialis, both of digit II and both of digit III — with I lateralis and IV medialis optional and interosseus IV lateralis and both of digit V not found at all, against the complete set of ten Kajava (1911) assembled from his variants. Gambaryan et al.'s Kajava correspondence is worth keeping: his flexores breves profundi radialis and ulnaris are the mediales and laterales here.

occurrences.name: Interossei
occurrences.origin: A complete set of ten, all by long tendons of which there are five: interossei I from the distal end of the prepollex; interossei II deeper from the same point and from intercarpal ligaments; interossei III from intercarpal ligaments; interossei IV and interosseus V medialis from intercarpal ligaments and the ulnare; interosseus V lateralis from the distal end of the pisiform.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxially (mediales) or postaxially (laterales) on the metacarpophalangeal joints of every digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **The full set of ten**, which Gambaryan et al. list among the features in which the platypus is more primitive than the echidnas, and one of which may even be the contrahens V. The tendon of the interosseus V medialis is shared with the interossei IV rather than with its own twin, which is an oddity of grouping rather than of position.

**Cunningham (1882) adds an independent observation of this layer in the same animal, and it is the layer that holds up when the others go.** He opened the platypus hand to check a sentence of Meckel's — that its interossei behave exactly like those of the foot, only thinner — and found the arrangement very different: the palmar adductors are reduced to one thread-like muscle and the dorsal interossei are absent, with only tough fibrous strands in the intermetacarpal spaces that may represent them, while **the flexores breves are well marked, each of two fleshy slips except that of the minimus, which has an ulnar head alone.** In the pes of the same animal these muscles are instead fused with the dorsal interossei to the point where the two layers must be separated from the dorsum before either can be read.

parts.name: Contrahens V
parts.note: Gambaryan et al. suggest one of the ten may be the contrahens V, without deciding which.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves profundi
occurrences.action: Flexes the metacarpophalangeal joints.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tawa hallae, Burch (2014). Insertion is the conserved end of this group — a single attachment to the ventral surface of the flexor process of the first phalanx of each digit in nearly every taxon studied, lying between the two distal tendons of the superficial layer. **The origin is a compromise between two states that may not be an ancestral condition at all**: lizards and turtles restrict these bellies to the distal carpal row, crocodylians involve both the distal carpals and each digit's metacarpal. Burch takes the crocodylian arrangement as the intermediate and most parsimonious reconstruction while flagging that the metacarpal origin may instead be convergent, acquired independently with the modified wrists of both modern archosaur clades — in which case the state reconstructed here for *Tawa* never existed.

The avian homologies underwriting the group are one muscle per digit: Adductor alulae for digit I, Abductor digiti majoris for digit II, Flexor digiti minoris — weak in most birds, a large fleshy belly in *Struthio* — for digit III.

occurrences.name: Interossei and the deep thenar and hypothenar muscles
occurrences.action: Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints; the interossei abduct and adduct the digits about the axis of digit III; the opponens muscles rotate the first and fifth metacarpals.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve, except the thenar muscles, which take the recurrent branch of the median nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **A large and openly contested carve-up, scored here on this record's own synonymy**, which already equates the deep short flexor layer with the mammalian interossei. Four dorsal interossei each from two adjacent metacarpal shafts; four palmar interossei from the palmar shafts of metacarpals 1, 2, 4 and 5; and the thenar and hypothenar short flexors and opponens muscles from the flexor retinaculum and the distal carpals. All insert on the proximal phalanges and, for the interossei, into the extensor expansion as well.

**The alternative assignments are real and are not settled here.** McMurrich, Howell and Lewis do not agree on how Interossei, Intermetacarpales, Dorsometacarpales and Contrahentes digitorum divide up, and Howell (1936) said as much. `intermetacarpales` and `dorsometacarpales` in this dataset both carry 'part of interossei dorsales' in their synonymy, so the human interossei have a claim on those two records as well; the rows there are scored uncertain and point back here rather than duplicating this one. The first palmar interosseus is often fused to the adductor pollicis, which is scored on `contrahentes-digitorum` — so the boundary between two of these records is, in a human, sometimes not a boundary.

**Dorsal interosseous** (Gest). Four bipennate muscles, each from two adjacent metacarpal shafts, to the proximal phalanx and extensor expansion — lateral side of digit 2, both sides of digit 3, medial side of digit 4. They abduct, which is what arising from two shafts and inserting on one side of one digit produces.

**Palmar interosseous** (Gest). Four unipennate muscles from the palmar shafts of metacarpals 1, 2, 4 and 5, to the proximal phalanx and extensor expansion on the side facing the third digit. The first is often fused with adductor pollicis, which is scored on `contrahentes-digitorum` — so one human muscle straddles the boundary between two records in this dataset, and Gest says so.

**Flexor pollicis brevis** (Gest). Flexor retinaculum and trapezium to the proximal phalanx of the thumb. Its superficial head is one of the two muscles the `flexores-breves-superficiales` row names as candidates for that layer, which is why that record is scored uncertain in a human rather than absent.

**Opponens pollicis** (Gest). Flexor retinaculum and trapezium to the shaft of the first metacarpal. It is the only thenar muscle that ends on a metacarpal rather than a phalanx, and rotating that metacarpal about its long axis is what opposition is.

**Flexor digiti minimi brevis** (Gest). Hook of the hamate and the flexor retinaculum to the proximal phalanx of the fifth digit.

**Opponens digiti minimi** (Gest). Hook of the hamate and the flexor retinaculum to the shaft of the fifth metacarpal. The hypothenar group repeats the thenar group muscle for muscle — abductor, short flexor, opponens — at the other edge of the hand.

occurrences.name: Mm. interossei ventrales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). A complex series of small muscles from the ligaments binding the carpals ventrally and from the metacarpal shafts, running proximolateral to distomesial — **opposed to the direction of the metacarpophalangeal ligaments they cross**. Digits I, II and III have a pair each, digit IV a single slip, and digit V none. Insertions are on the distal metacarpal and the proximal end of the first phalanx, with the lateral slips of digits II, III and IV giving rise to slender cylindrical tendons that run down the ventrolateral border of the digit to reach phalanges II and III. Scored on this record on McMurrich's equation, which Russell & Bauer reproduce: his M. flexor digitorum brevis profundus is their Mm. interossei ventrales.

occurrences.name: Mm. interossei volares
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Osawa's muscle 42, the deepest layer of the palm. Scored on this record on the same equation used for *Iguana*: Russell & Bauer's Mm. interossei ventrales are McMurrich's flexores digitorum breves profundi, which is this record's own synonymy.

occurrences.name: Intermediate group and dorsal interossei

parts.name: Flexores breves of the index, medius and annularis

occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura, which Cunningham describes first because it is the simplest. **The intermediate group is five muscles, one over the palmar aspect of each metacarpal**, and every one of them consists of two slips. In the thumb and little finger the two slips stay separate throughout — the flexor brevis pollicis from the second row of carpals, the flexor brevis minimi digiti with an ulnar head off the unciform and the retinaculum and a radial head deeper on the carpus — and each pair inserts one slip into each side of the base of the first phalanx, into bone only. The three middle muscles arise by a common tendon, part from the base of their own metacarpal and part from the palmar carpal ligaments, and divide half-way down; their slips insert **partly into bone and partly into the extensor tendon**, which is what lets them extend as well as flex. Cunningham draws the functional consequence himself: acting together the two slips flex at the metacarpophalangeal joint, acting singly they abduct or adduct, and that second action is best performed by the thumb and little finger muscles because their slips are unhampered by a common origin. The four dorsal interossei occupy the intermetacarpal spaces and have the same connections as in a human; **they are in no way connected with the intermediate muscles.**

occurrences.name: Intermediate group, dorsal interossei and opponens pollicis

parts.name: Accessory palmar slips of the dorsal interossei
Flexores breves of the index, medius and annularis

occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The intermediate group corresponds in all respects with the phascogale's. **The dorsal interossei are the interesting part**: four when the hand is viewed from the dorsum, but only the first and fourth act as abductors — the first onto the radial face of the index, the fourth onto the ulnar side of the ring finger, each partly into bone and partly into the extensor tendon. The second and third each end in a tendon that splits and inserts on the facing sides of two adjacent digits, so they approximate the three middle digits before extending them. Turn the hand over and each of the three ulnar interossei proves to have **an accessory palmar slip**, easily confounded with the intermediate muscles: two from either side of the base of the middle metacarpal, inserting one into each side of the base of its own first phalanx — the abductors of the middle finger — and a third from the base of the ring metacarpal to the ulnar side of the corresponding phalanx, an accessory abductor of the ring finger. The opponens pollicis survives only as a few fibres running from the conjoined abductor pollicis and radial flexor brevis pollicis to the metacarpal. Four dissections of this hand stand behind the description.

occurrences.name: Intermediate group, dorsal interossei and opponens minimi digiti

parts.name: Accessory palmar slips of the dorsal interossei
Flexores breves of the index, medius and annularis

occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Three of the four dorsal interossei have left the intermetacarpal spaces altogether and arise entirely from the dorsal surfaces of the metacarpals** — the second by two parts from the second and third, the third from the fourth, the fourth from the fourth and fifth. Only the first, the abductor indicis, is a single fleshy band, and it arises from the palmar surface of the base of the pollical metacarpal. They insert as in a human except the third, which like the thylacine's takes the two fingers it lies between. Cunningham then describes a mechanism: **the tendon of each of these muscles, the abductor indicis excepted, is tied by a little transverse fibrous band to the head of the neighbouring metacarpal**, holding it off the phalangeal base it acts on and so increasing its leverage. The same bands exist in the thylacine but are weak by comparison. The accessory palmar slips are present but less developed and differently placed than the thylacine's: an adductor of the index, an ulnar abductor of the middle finger, an abductor of the ring finger. The opponens minimi digiti is very distinct, fused with the ulnar part of the short flexor, and inserted into the lower half of the ulnar margin of the fifth metacarpal — continuous with that flexor's own insertion.

homology.notes: Universal, and the layer with the clearest mammalian continuation (the interossei). Note the boundary problem with the intermetacarpales — different authors assign the interossei to one, the other, or both.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 15 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexores breves profundi.

muscles.name: Lumbricales
muscles.developmental: Somitic; differentiate from the long digital flexor tendons.

consensus.origin: Tendons of the long digital flexor.
consensus.insertion: Extensor (dorsal) expansions of the digits.
consensus.action: Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints — the muscles that convert a claw grip into a flat grip.

occurrences.note: Absent in Ambystoma ordinarium, but McMurrich (1903a,b) reports lumbricales in other urodeles such as Ambystoma tigrinum.

occurrences.name: Lumbricales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Blotto et al. separate lumbricales breves (from distal carpal 3-4-5, inserting at the metacarpophalangeal joint) from lumbricales longi (from the tendines superficiales, in medial and lateral slips) — a distinction the amniote literature does not make.

occurrences.name: Lumbricales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator and Crocodylus, from Meers's descriptions. From the digital extensions of the common flexor digitorum longus tendon onto the extensor aspect of the metacarpophalangeal joints — so they flex the carpometacarpal joint and extend the metacarpophalangeal joint at the same time. Origin is tendon, not bone, as in every other taxon scored here.

occurrences.name: Lumbricals
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Four bellies for digits II-V, arising from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus at the level of the proximal metacarpals and inserting by thin tendons onto the medial base of the proximal, sometimes the middle, phalanges. Origin is tendon, not bone.

occurrences.name: Lumbricales
occurrences.origin: The dorsal (deep) side of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus immediately proximal to its branching. Lumbricales IV and V are always present and III is rare.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy or tendinous, always on the end of the preungual phalanx at its preaxial side.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Two muscles reliably, three at most, against four in the short-beaked echidna and three in the platypus.

occurrences.name: Lumbricales
occurrences.origin: Four muscles, lumbricales II-V, all from the dorsal side of the palmar sesamoid of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus; lumbricalis II is not always present.
occurrences.insertion: Preaxially at the end of the preungual phalanges of digits II-V. Lumbricales III and IV — and, per Fewkes (1877), V as well — bifurcate, each splitting off a preaxial head to the postaxial side of the preungual phalanx of the PRECEDING digit, so lumbricalis III supplies digits III and II, IV supplies IV and III, and V may supply V and IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. **The bifurcation is a very rare morphological condition**, reported elsewhere only in colugos (Panyutina et al. 2015), which bifurcate lumbricales III-V. It gives this series postaxial supply to digits II-IV, which the lumbricals of other tetrapods do not have.

occurrences.name: Lumbricales
occurrences.origin: Three muscles, from the dorsal side of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus at the distal border of its sesamoids: lumbricalis III from the medial sesamoid, IV from between the two, V from the lateral sesamoid.
occurrences.insertion: Thin sheet-like tendons running to the preaxial side of digits III-V, crossing the first interphalangeal joint without firm attachment onto the dorsum of the digit and fusing into the preaxial edge of the corresponding extensor digitorum communis tendon. Lumbricalis V fuses with the interosseus V medialis at the preaxial side of the metacarpophalangeal V joint on the way.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. A flexor-side muscle ending on an extensor tendon — the row records the phalanges it runs to, but the actual termination is on another muscle's tendon, which no osteological correlate would recover.

occurrences.name: Lumbricales
occurrences.note: Tawa hallae. Scored present and given no attachment rows on purpose. Burch (2014) considers lumbricales almost certainly present — they are in every taxon with a 'normal' manual morphology, and slips to at least digits II through IV are in all of his outgroups — but calls reconstructing their morphology too speculative to attempt. The variation is in exactly the two things an attachment row records: the number of slips, and where they end. They arise from the flexor digitorum longus tendons and/or the palmar aponeurosis, but insert on all digits (Haines 1950; Walker 1973; Abdala & Moro 2006) or only digits II-IV (Meers 2003; Russell & Bauer 2008), and on either the metacarpophalangeal or the proximal interphalangeal joint. There is no avian homolog to close the bracket. Presence is a safe inference from ubiquity; every row that would follow from it is not.

occurrences.name: Lumbricals
occurrences.action: Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints of digits 2-5.
occurrences.innervation: Median nerve to the radial two; deep branch of the ulnar nerve to the ulnar two.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables).
